div.head: Note on this Digital Edition
div.p: This publication is part of the research project «Teatro español y europeo de los siglos XVI y XVII: patrimonio y bases de datos», referencia PID2019-104045GB-C54 (acronym EMOTHE), funded by MICIN/AEI/10.13039/501100011033. This digital edition is an adaptation of the version of <<The Rover>> included in Montague Summers' 1915 anthology <<The Works of Mrs. Aphra Behn>> . All spelling and punctuation has been modernized using U.S. English spelling conventions, and all abbreviations (primarily found in the stage directions) have been expanded to represent their full meaning. All interventions made by Summers that do not appear in the original 1677 quarto have been marked in between brackets; any additional changes made by the TEI digital text editor have been marked with double brackets. For reference and citation purposes, this edition numbers speeches within each scene; for instance, the suggested reference form for the first speech in the play is 1.1.sp1.

div.head: PROLOGUE, Written by a Person of Quality
div.p: Wits, like physicians, never can agree When of a different society; And Rabel’s drops were never more cried down By all the learned doctors of the town Than a new play, whose author is unknown. Nor can those doctors with more malice sue (And powerful purses) the dissenting few Than those with an insulting pride do rail At all who are not of their own cabal. If a young poet hit your humor right, You judge him then out of revenge and spite; So amongst men there are ridiculous elves Who monkeys hate for being too like themselves, So that the reason of the grand debate, Why wit so oft is damned when good plays take, Is that you censure as you love or hate. Thus, like a learned conclave, poets sit Catholic judges both of sense and wit, And damn or save as they themselves think fit. Yet those who to others’ faults are so severe Are not so perfect but themselves may err. Some write correct indeed, but then the whole (Bating their own dull stuff i’th’ play) is stole: As bees do suck from flowers their honeydew, So they rob others striving to please you. Some write their characters genteel and fine, But then they do so toil for every line That what to you does easy seem, and plain Is the hard issue of their laboring brain. And some th’effects of all their pains we see Is but to mimic good <<extempore>> . Others by long converse about the town Have wit enough to write a leud lampoon, But their chief skill lies in a bawdy song. In short, the only wit that’s now in fashion Is but the gleanings of good conversation. As for the author of this coming play, I asked him what he thought fit I should say In thanks for your good company today: He called me fool, and said it was well known You came not here for our sakes but your own. New plays are stuffed with wits and with debauches, That crowd and sweat like cits in May-Day coaches.

div2.head: SCENE 1

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: What an impertinent thing is a young girl bred in a nunnery! How full of questions! Prithee no more, Hellena, I have told thee more than thou understandest already.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: The more’s my grief. I would fain know as much as you, which makes me so inquisitive; nor is’t enough to know you’re a lover, unless you tell me too, who ’tis you sigh for.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: When you are a lover, I’ll think you fit for a secret of that nature.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: ’Tis true, I was never a lover yet, but I begin to have a shrewd guess what ’tis to be so, and fancy it very pretty to sigh and sing, and blush and wish, and dream and wish, and long and wish to see the man. And when I do, look pale and tremble, just as you did when my brother brought home the fine English colonel to see you. What do you call him, Don Belvile?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Fie, Hellena!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: That blush betrays you, I am sure ’tis so! Or is it Don Antonio, the viceroy’s son? Or perhaps the rich old Don Vincentio, whom my father designs for your husband? Why do you blush again?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: With indignation! And how near soever my father thinks I am to marrying that hated object, I shall let him see I understand better what’s due to my beauty, birth and fortune, and more to my soul than to obey those unjust commands.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Now, hang me if I don’t love thee for that dear disobedience! I love mischief strangely, as most of our sex do, who are come to love nothing else. But tell me, dear Florinda, don’t you love that fine Anglese ? For I vow next to loving him myself, ’twill please me most that you do so, for he is so gay and so handsome.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Hellena, a maid designed for a nun ought not to be so curious in a discourse of love.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And dost thou think that ever I’ll be a nun? Or at least till I’m so old I’m fit for nothing else. Faith no, Sister! And that which makes me long to know whether you love Belvile is because I hope he has some mad companion or other that will spoil my devotion. Nay, I’m resolved to provide myself this carnival if there be e’er a handsome fellow of my humor above ground, though I ask first.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Prithee, be not so wild!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Now you have provided yourself with a man, you take no care for poor me! Prithee tell me, what dost thou see about me that is unfit for love? Have not I a world of youth? a humor gay? a beauty passable? a vigor desirable? well shaped, clean limbed, sweet breathed, and sense enough to know how all these ought to be employed to the best advantage? Yes, I do and will! Therefore lay aside your hopes of my fortune by my being a devotee, and tell me how you came acquainted with this Belvile, for I perceive you knew him before he came to Naples.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Yes, I knew him at the siege of Pamplona: he was then a colonel of French horse who, when the town was ransacked, nobly treated my brother and myself, preserving us from all insolences. And I must own (besides great obligations) I have I know not what that pleads kindly for him about my heart, and will suffer no other to enter. But see, my brother!

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro, Stephano, with a masking habit, and Callis

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Good morrow, sister. Pray, when saw you your lover, Don Vincentio?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I know not, Sir. Callis, when was he here? For I consider it so little, I know not when it was.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I have a command from my father here to tell you, you ought not to despise him, a man of so vast a fortune, and such a passion for you. Stephano, my things.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: A passion for me! ‘Tis more than e’er I saw or had a desire should be known! I hate Vincentio, and I would not have a man so dear to me as my brother follow the ill customs of our country and make a slave of his sister. And sir, my father’s will I’m sure you may divert.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I know not how dear I am to you, but I wish only to be ranked in your esteem equal with the English colonel Belvile – Why do you frown and blush? Is there any guilt belongs to the name of that cavalier?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I’ll not deny I value Belvile; when I was exposed to such dangers as the licensed lust of common soldiers threatened, when rage and conquest flew through the city, then Belvile — this criminal for my sake — threw himself into all dangers to save my honour. And will you not allow him my esteem?

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Yes, pay him what you will in honor, but you must consider Don Vincentio’s fortune and the jointure he’ll make you.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Let him consider my youth, beauty and fortune, which ought not to be thrown away on his age and jointure.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: ’Tis true, he’s not so young and fine a gentleman as that Belvile. But what jewels will that cavalier present you with? Those of his eyes and heart?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And are not those better than any Don Vincentio has brought from the Indies?

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Why, how now! Has your nunnery-breeding taught you to understand the value of hearts and eyes?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Better than to believe Vincentio deserves value from any woman! He may perhaps increase her bags, but not for family.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: This is fine! Go up to your devotion, you are not designed for the conversation of lovers.

p.seg: Nor saints yet a while, I hope.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: The girl’s mad! Is it a confinement to be carried into the country, to an ancient villa belonging to the family of the Vincentio’s these five hundred years, and have no other prospect than that pleasing one of seeing all her own that meets her eyes? A fine air, large fields and gardens, where she may walk and gather flowers?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: When, by moonlight? For I’m sure she dares not encounter with the heat of the sun; that were a task only for Don Vincentio and his Indian breeding, who loves it in the dog days. And if these be her daily divertissements, what are those of the night? To lie in a wide moth-eaten bedchamber with furniture in fashion in the reign of king Sancho the First, the bed that which his forefathers lived and died in.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: This apartment (new furbished and fitted out for the young wife) he (out of freedom) makes his dressing room. And being a frugal and a jealous coxcomb, instead of a valet to uncase his feeble carcass he desires you to do that office. Signs of favor, I’ll assure you, and such as you must not hope for unless your woman be out of the way.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Have you done yet?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: That honor being past, the giant stretches itself, yawns and sighs a belch or two as loud as a musket, throws himself into bed and expects you in his foul sheets; and e’er you can get yourself undressed, calls you with a snore or two. And are not these fine blessings to a young lady?

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Have you done yet?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And this man you must kiss, nay, you must kiss none but him too! and nuzzle through his beard to find his lips! and this you must submit to for threescore years, and all for a jointure.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: For all your character of Don Vincentio, she is as like to marry him as she was before.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Marry Don Vincentio! Hang me, such a wedlock would be worse than adultery with another man! I had rather see her in the Hostel de Dieu to waste her youth there in vows and be a handmaid to lazars and cripples than to lose it in such a marriage.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: You have considered, sister, that Belvile has no fortune to bring you to, is banished his country, despised at home, and pitied abroad?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: What then? the viceroy’s son is better than that old Sir Fisty. Don Vincentio! Don Indian! He thinks he’s trading to Gambo still, and would barter himself (that bell and bauble) for your youth and fortune.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Callis, take her hence and lock her up all this carnival, and at Lent she shall begin her everlasting penance in a monastery.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I care not, I had rather be a nun than be obliged to marry as you would have me, if I were designed for’t.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Do not fear the blessing of that choice: you shall be a nun.

p.seg: Shall I so? You may chance to be mistaken in my way of devotion. A nun! Yes, I am like to make a fine nun! I have an excellent humor for a grate. No, I’ll have a saint of my own to pray to shortly, if I like any that dares venture on me.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Callis, make it your business to watch this wild cat. As for you, Florinda, I’ve only tried you all this while and urged my father’s will, but mine is that you would love Antonio: he is brave and young, and all that can complete the happiness of a gallant maid. This absence of my father will give us opportunity to free you from Vincentio by marrying here, which you must do tomorrow.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Tomorrow!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Tomorrow, or ’twill be too late. ’Tis not my friendship to Antonio which makes me urge this but love to thee and hatred to Vincentio, therefore resolve upon’t tomorrow.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, I shall strive to do, as shall become your sister.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I’ll both believe and trust you, adieu.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: As become his sister! That is, to be as resolved your way as he is his.

lg.l: I ne’er till now perceived my ruin near,
I’ve no defense against Antonio’s love,
For he has all the advantages of nature,
The moving arguments of youth and fortune.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: But hark you, Callis, you will not be so cruel to lock me up indeed, will you?

sp.speaker: CALLIS
sp.p: I must obey the commands I hate; besides, do you consider what a life you are going to lead?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Yes, Callis, that of a nun, and till then I’ll be indebted a world of prayers to you if you let me now see what I never did: the divertissements of a carnival!

sp.speaker: CALLIS
sp.p: What, go in masquerade? ’Twill be a fine farewell to the world I take it. Pray, what would you do there?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: That which all the world does, as I am told: be as mad as the rest, and take all innocent freedom! Sister, you’ll go too, will you not? Come, prithee be not sad! We’ll outwit twenty brothers if you’ll be ruled by me. Come, put off this dull humor with your clothes, and assume one as gay and as fantastic as the dress my cousin Valeria and I have provided, and let’s ramble.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Callis, will you give us leave to go?

p.seg: I have a youthful itch of going myself!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Thou see’st my brother’s gone already, and thou shalt attend and watch us.

sp.speaker: STEPHANO
sp.p: Madam, the habits are come, and your cousin Valeria is dressed and stays for you.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: ’Tis well! I’ll write a note, and if I chance to see Belvile and want an opportunity to speak to him, that shall let him know what I’ve resolved in favor of him.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Come, let’s in and dress us.

div2.head: SCENE 2
div2.stage: Enter Belvile, melancholy, Blunt and Frederick

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Why, what the devil ails the colonel, in a time when all the world is gay, to look like mere Lent thus? Hadst thou been long enough in Naples to have been in love, I should have sworn some such judgment had befallen thee.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: No, I have made no new amours since I came to Naples.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: You have left none behind you in Paris.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Neither.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I can’t divine the cause then, unless the old cause: the want of money.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: And another old cause: the want of a wench. Would not that revive you?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: You’re mistaken, Ned.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Nay, ’sheartlikins, then thou art past cure.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I have found it out: thou hast renewed thy acquaintance with the lady that cost thee so many sighs at the siege of Pamplona. Pox on’t, what d’ye call her – her brother’s a noble Spaniard – nephew to the dead general – Florinda! Ay, Florinda! And will nothing serve thy turn but that damned virtuous woman, whom on my conscience thou lovest in spite too, because thou seest little or no possibility of gaining her?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Thou art mistaken, I have interest enough in that lovely virgin’s heart to make me proud and vain, were it not abated by the severity of a brother, who perceiving my happiness –

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Has civilly forbid thee the house?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: ’Tis so, to make way for a powerful rival, the viceroy’s son, who has the advantage of me in being a man of fortune, a Spaniard, and her brother’s friend, which gives him liberty to make his court whilst I have recourse only to letters and distant looks from her window, which are as soft and kind as those which Heaven sends down on penitents.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Hey day! ’Sheartlikins, simile! By this light the man is quite spoiled. Frederick, what the devil are we made of that we cannot be thus concerned for a wench? ’Sheartlikins, our cupids are like the cooks of the camp: they can roast or boil a woman, but they have none of the fine tricks to set ’em off, no hogoes to make the sauce pleasant and the stomach sharp.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I dare swear I have had a hundred as young, kind and handsome as this Florinda, and dogs eat me if they were not as troublesome to me i’th’ morning as they were welcome o’er night.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: And yet, I warrant, he would not touch another woman if he might have her for nothing.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: That’s thy joy, a cheap whore.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Why, ’sheartlikins, I love a frank soul! When did you ever hear of an honest woman that took a man’s money? I warrant ’em good ones. But, gentlemen, you may be free, you have been kept so poor with parliaments and protectors that the little stock you have is not worth preserving, but I thank my stars I have more grace than to forfeit my estate by cavaliering.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Methinks only following the court should be sufficient to entitle ’em to that.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, they know I follow it to do it no good, unless they pick a hole in my coat for lending you money now and then, which is a greater crime to my conscience, gentlemen, than to the Commonwealth.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ha! Dear Belvile! Noble Colonel!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Willmore! welcome ashore, my dear rover! What happy wind blew us this good fortune?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Let me salute you my dear Fred, and then command me. How is’t, honest lad?

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Faith, sir, the old complement, infinitely the better to see my dear mad Willmore again! Prithee, why camest thou ashore? And where’s the prince?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: He’s well, and reigns still lord of the watery element. I must aboard again within a day or two, and my business ashore was only to enjoy myself a little this carnival.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Pray know our new friend, sir. He’s but bashful, a raw traveler, but honest, stout, and one of us.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: That you esteem him gives him an interest here.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Your servant, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: But well! Faith, I’m glad to meet you again in a warm climate, where the kind sun has its god-like power still over the wine and woman. Love and mirth are my business in Naples, and if I mistake not the place, here’s an excellent market for chapmen of my humor.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: See, here be those kind merchants of love you look for.

div2.stage: Enter several men in masking habits, some playing on music, others dancing after; women dressed like courtesans, with papers pinned to their breasts and baskets of flowers in their hands

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, what have we here!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Now the game begins.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Fine pretty creatures! May a stranger have leave to look and love? What’s here – (Reads the paper) “Roses for every month”!

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: “Roses for every month.” What means that?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: They are, or would have you think they’re courtesans, who here in Naples are to be hired by the month.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Kind and obliging to inform us! Pray, where do these roses grow? I would fain plant some of ’em in a bed of mine.

sp.speaker: WOMAN
sp.p: Beware such roses, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A pox of fear! I’ll be baked with thee between a pair of sheets, and that’s thy proper still, so I might but strow such roses over me and under me. Fair one, would you would give me leave to gather at your bush this idle month, I would go near to make some body smell of it all the year after.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: And thou hast need of such a remedy, for thou stinkest of tar and rope-ends like a dock or pesthouse.

div2.stage: The woman puts herself into the hands of a man, and exit

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, nay, you shall not leave me so!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: By all means, use no violence here!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Death! Just as I was going to be damnably in love, to have her led off! I could pluck that rose out of his hand, and even kiss the bed, the bush it grew in.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: No friend to love like a long voyage at sea.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Except a nunnery, Fred.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Death! But will they not be kind, quickly be kind? Thou knowst I’m no tame sigher, but a rampant lion of the forest.

div2.stage: Two men dressed all over with horns of several sorts, making grimaces at one another, with papers pinned on their backs, advance from the farther end of the scene

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Oh the fantastical rogues, how they are dressed! ’Tis a satire against the whole sex.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Is this a fruit that grows in this warm country?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Yes: ’tis pretty to see these Italian start, swell, and stab at the word ‘cuckold,’ and yet stumble at horns on every threshold.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: See what’s on their back: (Reads) “Flowers for every night.” Ah, rogue! And more sweet than roses of every month! This is a gardener of Adam’s own breeding.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What think you of those grave people? Is a wake in Essex half so mad or extravagant?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I like their sober grave way, ’tis a kind of legal authorized fornication, where the men are not chid for’t, nor the women despised, as amongst our dull English; even the monsieurs want that part of good manners.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: But here in Italy a monsieur is the humblest best-bred gentleman; duels are so baffled by bravos that an age shews not one but between a Frenchman and a hangman, who is as much too hard for him on the piazza as they are for a Dutchman on the New Bridge. But see, another crew.

div2.stage: Enter Florinda, Hellena, and Valeria, dressed like gypsies; Callis and Stephano, Lucetta, Phillippo and Sancho in masquerade

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Sister, there’s your Englishman, and with him a handsome proper fellow. I’ll to him, and instead of telling him his fortune, try my own.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Gypsies, on my life! Sure these will prattle if a man cross their hands. (Goes to Hellena) Dear pretty (and I hope) young devil, will you tell an amorous stranger what luck he’s like to have?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Have a care how you venture with me, sir, lest I pick your pocket, which will more vex your English humor than an Italian fortune will please you.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How the devil camest thou to know my country and humour?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: The first I guess by a certain forward impudence, which does not displease me at this time; and the loss of your money will vex you because I hope you have but very little to lose.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad child, thou’rt i’th’ right: it is so little I dare not offer it thee for a kindness. But cannot you divine what other things of more value I have about me that I would more willingly part with?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Indeed no, that’s the business of a witch, and I am but a gypsy yet. Yet, without looking in your hand, I have a parlous guess ’tis some foolish heart you mean, an inconstant English heart as little worth stealing as your purse.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, then thou dost deal with the devil, that’s certain! Thou hast guessed as right as if thou hadst been one of that number it has languished for. I find you’ll be better acquainted with it. Nor can you take it in a better time, for I am come from sea, child, and Venus not being propitious to me in her own element, I have a world of love in store. Would you would be good-natured and take some on’t off my hands?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Why, I could be inclined that way, but for a foolish vow I am going to make – to die a maid.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Then thou art damned without redemption, and as I am a good Christian I ought in charity to divert so wicked a design. Therefore prithee, dear creature, let me know quickly when and where I shall begin to set a helping hand to so good a work.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: If you should prevail with my tender heart (as I begin to fear you will, for you have horrible loving eyes) there will be difficulty in’t that you’ll hardly undergo for my sake.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, child, I have been bred in dangers, and wear a sword that has been employed in a worse cause than for a handsome kind woman. Name the danger: let it be anything but a long siege, and I’ll undertake it.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Can you storm?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh, most furiously.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: What think you of a nunnery wall? For he that wins me, must gain that first.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A nun! Oh, how I love thee for’t! There’s no sinner like a young saint. Nay, now there’s no denying me: the old law had no curse (to a woman) like dying a maid; witness Jephthah’s daughter.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: A very good text this, if well handled. And I perceive, Father Captain, you would impose no severe penance on her who was inclined to console herself before she took orders.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: If she be young and handsome.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Ay, there’s it, but if she be not –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: By this hand, child, I have an implicit faith and dare venture on thee with all faults. Besides, ’tis more meritorious to leave the world when thou hast tasted and proved the pleasure on’t; then ’twill be a virtue in thee, which now will be pure ignorance.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I perceive, good Father Captain, you design only to make me fit for Heaven. But, if on the contrary you should quite divert me from it and bring me back to the world again, I should have a new man to seek, I find, and what a grief that will be – for when I begin, I fancy I shall love like anything. I never tried yet.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, and that’s kind! Prithee, dear creature, give me credit for a heart, for faith, I’m a very honest fellow. Oh, I long to come first to the banquet of love, and such a swinging appetite I bring – Oh, I’m impatient! Thy lodging, sweetheart, thy lodging or I’m a dead man!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Why must we be either guilty of fornication or murder if we converse with you men? And is there no difference between leave to love me, and leave to lie with me?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, child, they were made to go together.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: (Pointing to Blunt) Are you sure this is the man?

sp.speaker: SANCHO
sp.p: When did I mistake your game?

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: This is a stranger, I know by his gazing. If he be brisk, he’ll venture to follow me; and then, if I understand my trade, he’s mine. He’s English too, and they say that’s a sort of good-natured loving people, and have generally so kind an opinion of themselves that a woman with any wit may flatter ’em into any sort of fool she pleases.

div2.stage: She often passes by Blunt and gazes on him; he struts, and cocks, and walks, and gazes on her

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Tis so, she is taken! I have beauties which my false glass at home did not discover.

p.seg: This woman watches me so, I shall get no opportunity to discover myself to him, and so miss the intent of my coming.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I thought how right you guessed: all men are in love, or pretend to be so. (Walks away) Come, let me go, I’m weary of this fooling.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I will not, till you have confessed whether the passion that you have vowed Florinda be true or false.

div2.stage: She holds him, he strives to get from her

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: (Turns quick towards her) Florinda!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Softly.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Thou hast named one will fix me here forever.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: She’ll be disappointed, then, who expects you this night at the garden gate, and if you’ll fail not – as let me see the other hand – you will go near to do. She vows to die or make you happy.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What canst thou mean?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: That which I say. Farewell.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Oh charming sybil, stay, complete that joy which as it is will turn into distraction! Where must I be? At the garden gate? I know it – at night you say – I’ll sooner forfeit Heaven than disobey.

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro and other maskers, and pass over the stage

sp.speaker: CALLIS
sp.p: Madam, your brother’s here.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Take this to instruct you farther.

div2.stage: Gives him a letter, and goes off

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Have a care, sir, what you promise: this may be a trap laid by her brother to ruin you.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Do not disturb my happiness with doubts.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: My dear pretty creature, a thousand blessings on thee. Still in this habit, you say, and after dinner at this place.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Yes, if you will swear to keep your heart and not bestow it between this time and that.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: By all the little gods of love I swear, I’ll leave it with you. And if you run away with it, those deities of justice will revenge me.

div2.stage: Exit all the women except Lucetta

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Do you know the hand?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: ’Tis Florinda’s! All blessings fall upon the virtuous maid.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Nay, no idolatry, a sober sacrifice I’ll allow you.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Oh friends! The welcomest news, the softest letter! Nay, you shall see it, and could you now be serious I might be made the happiest man the sun shines on.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: The reason of this mighty joy?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: See how kindly she invites me to deliver her from the threatened violence of her brother. Will you not assist me?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I know not what thou meanest, but I’ll make one at any mischief where a woman’s concerned. But she’ll be grateful to us for the favor, will she not?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: How mean you?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How should I mean? Thou knowest there’s but one way for a woman to oblige me.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Don’t prophane, the maid is nicely virtuous.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Who pox, then she’s fit for nothing but a husband. Let her e’en go, colonel.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Peace, she’s the colonel’s mistress, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Let her be the devil: if she be thy mistress, I’ll serve her. Name the way.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Read here this postscript.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: (Reads) “At ten at night, at the garden gate – of which, if I cannot get the key, I will contrive a way over the wall; come attended with a friend or two.” Kind heart, if we three cannot weave a string to let her down a garden wall,’twere pity but the hangman wove one for us all.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Let her alone for that: your woman’s wit, your fair kind woman, will outtrick a brother or a Jew and contrive like a Jesuit in chains. But see, Ned Blunt is stolen out after the lure of a damsel!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: So he’ll scarce find his way home again unless we get him cried by the bellman in the marketplace, and ’twould sound prettily: a lost English boy of thirty.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I hope ’tis some common crafty sinner, one that will fit him. It may be she’ll sell him for Peru, the rogue’s sturdy and would work well in a mine. At least I hope she’ll dress him for our mirth, cheat him of all, then have him well-favoredly banged, and turned out naked at midnight.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Prithee, what humor is he of, that you wish him so well?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Why, of an English elder brother’s humor: educated in a nursery with a maid to tend him till fifteen, and lies with his grandmother till he’s of age; one that knows no pleasure beyond riding to the next fair or going up to London with his right worshipful father in parliament time, wearing gay clothes or making honorable love to his lady mother’s laundry maid; gets drunk at a hunting match, and ten to one then gives some proofs of his prowess. A pox upon him! He’s our banker and has all our cash about him, and if he fail we are all broke.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Oh let him alone for that matter, he’s of a damned stingy quality, that will secure our stock. I know not in what danger it were indeed, if the jilt should pretend she’s in love with him, for ’tis a kind believing coxcomb. Otherwise, if he part with more than a piece of eight, geld him; for which offer he may chance to be beaten, if she be a whore of the first rank.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Nay, the rogue will not be easily beaten, he’s stout enough. Perhaps if they talk beyond his capacity he may chance to exercise his courage upon some of them. Else I’m sure they’ll find it as difficult to beat as to please him.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: ’Tis a lucky devil to light upon so kind a wench!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Thou hadst a great deal of talk with thy little gypsy, couldst thou do no good upon her? For mine was hard-hearted.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Hang her, she was some damned honest person of quality, I’m sure, she was so very free and witty. If her face be but answerable to her wit and humor, I would be bound to constancy this month to gain her. In the meantime, have you made no kind acquaintance since you came to town? You do not use to be honest so long, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Faith, love has kept us honest, we have been all fired with a beauty newly come to town: the famous Paduana Angellica Bianca.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What, the mistress of the dead Spanish general?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Yes, she’s now the only adored beauty of all the youth in Naples, who put on all their charms to appear lovely in her sight: their coaches, liveries, and themselves all gay as on a monarch’s birthday, to attract the eyes of this fair charmer while she has the pleasure to behold all languish for her that see her.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: ’Tis pretty to see with how much love the men regard her, and how much envy the women.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What gallant has she?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: None, she’s exposed to sale, and four days in the week she’s yours, for so much a month.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: The very thought of it quenches all manner of fire in me. Yet prithee, let’s see her.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Let’s first to dinner, and after that we’ll pass the day as you please. But at night ye must all be at my devotion.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I will not fail you.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Enter Belvile and Frederick in masking habits, and Willmore in his own clothes with a vizard in his hand

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: But why thus disguised and muzzled?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Because whatever extravagances we commit in these faces, our own may not be obliged to answer ’em.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I should have changed my eternal buff too: but no matter, my little gypsy would not have found me out then, for if she should change hers it is impossible I should know her unless I should hear her prattle. A pox on’t, I cannot get her out of my head! Pray heaven if ever I do see her again, she prove damnable ugly that I may fortify myself against her tongue.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Have a care of love, for o’ my conscience she was not of a quality to give thee any hopes.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Pox on ’em, why do they draw a man in then? She has played with my heart so, that ’twill never lie still till I have met with some kind wench that will play the game out with me! Oh, for my arms full of soft, white, kind woman such as I fancy Angellica.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: This is her house, if you were but in stock to get admittance. They have not dined yet: I perceive the picture is not out.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I long to see the shadow of the fair substance, a man may gaze on that for nothing.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Colonel, thy hand – and thine, Fred. I have been an ass, a deluded fool, a very coxcomb from my birth till this hour, and heartily repent my little faith.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What the devil’s the matter with thee, Ned?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Oh such a mistress, Fred, such a girl!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ha! Where?

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Ay, where?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: So fond, so amorous, so toying and fine! And all for sheer love, ye rogue! Oh how she looked and kissed! And soothed my heart from my bosom! I cannot think I was awake, and yet methinks I see and feel her charms still! Fred, try if she have not left the taste of her balmy kisses upon my lips –

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Death, man, where is she?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: What a dog was I to stay in dull England so long! How have I laughed at the colonel when he sighed for love! But now the little archer has revenged him, and by his own dart I can guess at all his joys which then I took for fancies, mere dreams and fables – Well, I’m resolved to sell all in Essex and plant here forever.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What a blessing ’tis thou hast a mistress thou darest boast of, for I know thy humor is rather to have a proclaimed clap than a secret amour.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Dost know her name?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Her name? No, ’sheartlikins: what care I for names? She’s fair, young, brisk and kind, even to ravishment; and what a pox care I for knowing her by another title?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Didst give her anything?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Give her! Ha, ha, ha! Why, she’s a person of quality! That’s a good one, ‘give her’! ’Sheartlikins, dost think such creatures are to be bought? Or are we provided for such a purchase? Give her, quoth ye? Why, she presented me with this bracelet for the toy of a diamond I used to wear! No, gentlemen, Ned Blunt is not everybody – she expects me again tonight.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad that’s well; we’ll all go.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Not a soul: no, gentlemen, you are wits; I am a dull country rogue, I.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Well, Sir, for all your person of quality I shall be very glad to understand your purse be secure: ’tis our whole estate at present, which we are loath to hazard in one bottom. Come, sir, unload.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Take the necessary trifle, useless now to me, that am beloved by such a gentlewoman. ’Sheartlikins, money! Here, take mine too.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: No, keep that to be cozened, that we may laugh.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Cozened! Death! Would I could meet with one that would cozen me of all the love I could spare tonight.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Pox, ’tis some common whore, upon my life.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: A whore! Yes, with such clothes! Such jewels! Such a house! Such furniture, and so attended! A whore!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Why yes, sir, they are whores, though they’ll neither entertain you with drinking, swearing, or bawdy; are whores in all those gay clothes and right jewels; are whores with great houses richly furnished with velvet beds, store of plate, handsome attendance, and fine coaches; are whores, and errant ones.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Pox on’t, where do these fine whores live?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Where no rogue in office yclept constables dare give ’em laws, nor the wine-inspired bullies of the town break their windows; yet they are whores, though this Essex calf believe them persons of quality.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, y’are all fools, there are things about this Essex calf that shall take with the ladies beyond all your wits and parts! This shape and size, gentlemen, are not to be despised; my waist tolerably long, with other inviting signs that shall be nameless.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, I believe he may have met with some person of quality that may be kind to him.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Dost thou perceive any such tempting things about him, should make a fine woman – and of quality – pick him out from all mankind to throw away her youth and beauty upon, nay, and her dear heart too? No, no, Angellica has raised the price too high.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: May she languish for mankind till she die, and be damned for that one sin alone.

div2.stage: Enter two bravos, and hang up a great picture of Angellica’s against the balcony, and two little ones at each side of the door

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: See there the fair sign to the inn, where a man may lodge that’s fool enough to give her price.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, gentlemen, what’s this?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: A famous courtesan that’s to be sold.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: A how! To be sold! Nay, then I have nothing to say to her – Sold! What impudence is practiced in this country? With order and decency whoring’s established here by virtue of the Inquisition! Come let’s be gone, I’m sure we’re no chapmen for this commodity.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Thou art none, I’m sure, unless thou couldst have her in thy bed at the price of a coach in the street.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How wondrous fair she is – a thousand crowns a month, by Heaven as many kingdoms were too little! A plague of this poverty, of which I ne’er complain but when it hinders my approach to beauty, which virtue ne’er could purchase.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: What’s this? (Reads) “A thousand crowns a month.” ’Sheartlikins, here’s a sum! Sure ’tis a mistake. Hark you, friend, does she take or give so much by the month!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: A thousand crowns! Why, ’tis a portion for the infanta .

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Hark ye, friends, won’t she trust?

sp.speaker: BRAVO
sp.p: This is a trade, sir, that cannot live by credit.

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro in masquerade, followed by Stephano

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: See, here’s more company, let’s walk off a while.

div2.stage: Enter Angelica and Moretta in the balcony, and draw a silk curtain

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Fetch me a thousand crowns, I never wish to buy this beauty at an easier rate.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Prithee what said those fellows to thee?

sp.speaker: BRAVO
sp.p: Madam, the first were admirers of beauty only, but no purchasers; they were merry with your price and picture, laughed at the sum, and so passed off.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: No matter, I’m not displeased with their rallying: their wonder feeds my vanity, and he that wishes to buy gives me more pride than he that gives my price can make me pleasure.

sp.speaker: BRAVO
sp.p: Madam, the last I knew through all his disguises to be Don Pedro, nephew to the general, and who was with him in Pamplona.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Don Pedro! My old gallant’s nephew! When his uncle died he left him a vast sum of money; it is he who was so in love with me at Padua and who used to make the general so jealous.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Is this he that used to prance before our window and take such care to shew himself an amorous ass? If I am not mistaken, he is the likeliest man to give your price.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: The man is brave and generous, but of an humor so uneasy and inconstant, that the victory over his heart is as soon lost as won, a slave that can add little to the triumph of the conqueror. But inconstancy’s the sin of all mankind, therefore I’m resolved that nothing but gold shall charm my heart.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: I’m glad on’t, ’tis only interest that women of our profession ought to consider; though I wonder what has kept you from that general disease of our sex so long – I mean that of being in love.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: A kind but sullen star, under which I had the happiness to be born. Yet I have had no time for love, the bravest and noblest of mankind have purchased my favors at so dear a rate as if no coin but gold were current with our trade. But here’s Don Pedro again: fetch me my lute, for ’tis for him or Don Antonio the viceroy’s son that I have spread my nets.

div2.stage: Enter at one door Don Pedro, and Stephano; Don Antonio and Diego [his page] at the other door, with people following him in masquerade antiquely attired, some with music; they both go up to the picture

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: A thousand crowns! Had not the painter flattered her, I should not think it dear.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Flattered her! By Heaven, he cannot. I have seen the original, nor is there one charm here more than adorns her face and eyes; all this soft and sweet, with a certain languishing air, that no artist can represent.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: What I heard of her beauty before had fired my soul, but this confirmation of it has blown it into a flame.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: DIEGO
sp.p: Sir, I have known you throw away a thousand crowns on a worse face, and though y’are near your marriage, you may venture a little love here. Florinda will not miss it.

p.seg: Ha! Florinda! Sure ’tis Antonio.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Florinda! Name not those distant joys, there’s not one thought of her will check my passion here.

p.seg: Florinda scorned! And all my hopes defeated of the possession of Angellica!

lg.l: When Damon first began to love,
He languished in a soft desire,
And knew not how the gods to move,
To lessen or increase his fire,
For Celia in her charming eyes
Wore all love’s sweet, and all his cruelties.
But as beneath a shade he lay,
Weaving of flowers for Celia’s hair,
She chanced to lead her flock that way,
And saw the am’rous shepherd there.
She gazed around upon the place,
And saw the grove (resembling night)
To all the joys of love invite,
Whilst guilty smiles and blushes dressed her face.
At this the bashful youth all transport grew,
And with kind force he taught the virgin how
To yield what all his sighs could never do.

div2.stage: Angellica throws open the curtains and bows to Antonio, who pulls off his vizard and bows and blows up kisses; Pedro, unseen, looks in his face

lg.l: By Heaven, she’s charming fair!
’Tis he, the false Antonio!
(To the bravo) Friend, where must I pay my offering of love?
My thousand crowns, I mean.
That offering I have designed to make,
And yours will come too late.
Prithee be gone, I shall grow angry else,
And then thou art not safe.
My anger may be fatal, sir, as yours,
And he that enters here may prove this truth.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I know not who thou art, but I am sure thou’rt worth my killing and aiming at Angellica.

div2.stage: Enter Willmore and Blunt, who draw and part ’em

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, here’s fine doings.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Tilting for the wench, I’m sure. Nay gad, if that would win her I have as good a sword as the best of ye. Put up, put up, and take another time and place for this is designed for lovers only.

lg.l: We are prevented; dare you meet me tomorrow on the Molo?
For I’ve a title to a better quarrel,
That of Florinda, in whose credulous heart
Thou’st made an interest, and destroyed my hopes.
Dare?
I’ll meet thee there as early as the day.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: We will come thus disguised, that whosoever chance to get the better he may escape unknown.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: It shall be so. [Exit Pedro and Stephano] Who should this rival be? Unless the English colonel of whom I’ve often heard Don Pedro speak; it must be he, and time he were removed who lays a claim to all my happiness.

div2.stage: Willmore, having gazed all this while on the picture, pulls down a little one

lg.l: This posture’s loose and negligent,
The sight on’t would beget a warm desire
In souls, whom impotence and age had chilled.
This must along with me.

sp.speaker: BRAVO
sp.p: What means this rudeness, sir? Restore the picture.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Ha! Rudeness committed to the fair Angellica! Restore the picture, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Indeed I will not, sir.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: By Heaven, but you shall.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, do not show your sword: if you do, by this dear beauty I will show mine too.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: What right can you pretend to’t?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: That of possession which I will maintain. You, perhaps, have 1000 crowns to give for the original.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: No matter, Sir, you shall restore the Picture.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Oh, Moretta! What’s the matter?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Or leave your life behind.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Death! You lie, I will do neither.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Hold, I command you, if for me you fight.

div2.stage: They fight, the Spaniards join with Antonio, Blunt laying on like mad; they leave off and bow

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How heavenly fair she is! Ah plague of her price.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: You sir in buff, you that appear a soldier, that first began this insolence.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: ’Tis true, I did so, if you call it insolence for a man to preserve himself. I saw your charming picture and was wounded, quite through my soul each pointed beauty ran, and wanting a thousand crowns to procure my remedy I laid this little picture to my bosom – which, if you cannot allow me, I’ll resign.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: No, you may keep the trifle.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: You shall first ask my leave, and this.

div2.stage: Enter Belvile and Frederick who join with the English

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Hold! Will you ruin me? Biskey, Sebastian, part them!

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Oh madam, we’re undone, a pox upon that rude fellow, he’s set on to ruin us; we shall never see good days till all these fighting poor rogues are sent to the galleys.

div2.stage: Enter Belvile, Blunt and Willmore, with his shirt bloody

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, beat me at this sport and I’ll ne’er wear sword more.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: (To Willmore) The devil’s in thee for a mad fellow, thou art always one at an unlucky adventure. Come, let’s be gone whilst we’re safe, and remember these are Spaniards, a sort of people that know how to revenge an affront.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: You bleed; I hope you are not wounded.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Not much; a plague upon your dons , if they fight no better they’ll ne’er recover Flanders. What the devil was’t to them that I took down the picture?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Took it! ’Sheartlikins, we’ll have the great one too, ’tis ours by conquest. Prithee, help me up, and I’ll pull it down.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Stay, sir, and e’er you affront me further let me know how you durst commit this outrage. To you I speak, sir, for you appear like a gentleman.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: To me, madam? Gentlemen, your servant.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Is the Devil in thee? Dost know the danger of entering the house of an incensed courtesan?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I thank you for your care, but there are other matters in hand, there are, though we have no great temptation. Death! Let me go.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Yes, to your lodging if you will, but not in here. Damn these gay harlots, by this hand I’ll have as sound and handsome a whore for a patacoon. Death, man, she’ll murder thee.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh! Fear me not, shall I not venture where a beauty calls? A lovely charming beauty? For fear of danger! When by Heaven there’s none so great as to long for her, whilst I want money to purchase her.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Therefore ’tis loss of time unless you had the thousand crowns to pay.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: It may be she may give a favor, at least I shall have the pleasure of saluting her when I enter and when I depart.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Pox, she’ll as soon lie with thee as kiss thee, and sooner stab than do either; you shall not go.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Fear not, sir, all I have to wound with is my eyes.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Let him go, ’sheartlikins, I believe the gentlewoman means well.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Well, take thy fortune; we’ll expect you in the next street. Farewell, fool, farewell.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Bye, colonel.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: The rogue’s stark mad for a wench.

div2.head: SCENE 2

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Insolent sir, how durst you pull down my picture?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Rather, how durst you set it up, to tempt poor amorous mortals with so much excellence, which I find you have but too well consulted by the unmerciful price you set upon’t? Is all this heaven of beauty shown to move despair in those that cannot buy? And can you think the effects of that despair should be less extravagant than I have shown?

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I sent for you to ask my pardon, sir, not to aggravate your crime. I thought I should have seen you at my feet imploring it.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: You are deceived, I came to rail at you, and talk such truths, too, as shall let you see the vanity of that pride which taught you how to set such a price on sin. For such it is, whilst that which is love’s due is meanly bartered for.

p.seg: – and guess my business

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: He knows himself of old, I believe those breeches and he have been acquainted ever since he was beaten at Worcester.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Nay, do not abuse the poor creature.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Good weather-beaten corporal, will you march off? We have no need of your doctrine, though you have of our charity; but at present we have no scraps, we can afford no kindness for God’s sake; in fine, sirrah, the price is too high i’th’ mouth for you, therefore troop, I say.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Here, good forewoman of the shop, serve me, and I’ll be gone.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Keep it to pay your laundress, your linen stinks of the gun room, for here’s no selling by retail.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Thou hast sold plenty of thy stale ware at a cheap rate.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Ay, the more silly kind heart I, but this is an age wherein beauty is at higher rates. In fine, you know the price of this.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I grant you ’tis here set down a thousand crowns a month. Bawd, take your black lead and sum it up that I may have a pistole-worth of these vain gay things, and I’ll trouble you no more.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Pox on him, he’ll fret me to death: abominable fellow, I tell thee, we only sell by the whole piece.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: ’Tis very hard, the whole cargo or nothing. Faith, madam, my stock will not reach it, I cannot be your chapman. Yet I have countrymen in town, merchants of love like me; I’ll see if they’ll put for a share, we cannot lose much by it, and what we have no use for we’ll sell upon the Friday’s Mart at “Who gives more?”. I am studying, madam, how to purchase you, though at present I am unprovided of money.

p.seg: Sure, this from any other man would anger me, nor shall he know the conquest he has made.

lg.l: Yes, I am poor, but I’m a gentleman,
And one that scorns this baseness which you practice.
Poor as I am, I would not sell myself,
No, not to gain your charming high-prized person.
Though I admire you strangely for your beauty,
Yet I condemn your mind.
And yet I would at any rate enjoy you;
At your own rate – but cannot – See here
The only sum I can command on earth:
I know not where to eat when this is gone,
Yet such a slave I am to love and beauty,
This last reserve I’ll sacrifice to enjoy you.
Nay, do not frown, I know you are to be bought,
And would be bought by me, by me,
For a mean trifling sum, if I could pay it down.
Which happy knowledge I will still repeat,
And lay it to my heart, it has a virtue in’t,
And soon will cure those wounds your eyes have made.
And yet – there’s something so divinely powerful there –
Nay, I will gaze – to let you see my strength.
lg.stage: (Holds her, looks on her, and pauses and sighs)
lg.l: By Heaven, bright creature, I would not for the world
Thy fame were half so fair as is thy face.

l.seg: His words go through me to the very soul.

lg.l: [To Willmore] If you have nothing else to say to me.
Yes, you shall hear how infamous you are –
For which I do not hate thee –
But that secures my heart, and all the flames it feels
Are but so many lusts:
I know it by their sudden bold intrusion.
The fire’s impatient and betrays, ’tis false,
For had it been the purer flame of love,
I should have pined and languished at your feet,
Ere found the impudence to have discovered it.
I now dare stand your scorn and your denial.

p.seg: Sure she’s bewitched, that she can stand thus tamely and hear his saucy railing.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: [To Moretta] How dare you take this liberty? Withdraw! Pray, tell me, sir, are not you guilty of the same mercenary crime? When a lady is proposed to you for a wife, you never ask how fair, discreet, or virtuous she is, but what’s her fortune – which if but small, you cry “she will not do my business” and basely leave her though she languish for you. Say, is not this as poor?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: It is a barbarous custom, which I will scorn to defend in our sex, and do despise in yours.

lg.l: Thou art a brave fellow! Put up thy gold, and know,
That were thy fortune large as is thy soul,
Thou shouldst not buy my love,
Couldst thou forget those mean effects of vanity
Which set me out to sale; and as a lover, prize
My yielding joys.
Canst thou believe they’ll be entirely thine,
Without considering they were mercenary?

p.seg: Ha, death, I’m going to believe her!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Prithee, confirm that faith – or if thou canst not – flatter me a little, ’twill please me from thy mouth.

l.seg: Curse on thy charming tongue! Dost thou return
My feigned contempt with so much subtlety?

lg.l: Thou’st found the easiest way into my heart,
Though I yet know that all thou sayest is false.

div2.stage: Turning from her in a rage

lg.l: By all that’s good ’tis real,
I never loved before, though oft a mistress.
Shall my first vows be slighted?

l.seg: What can she mean?

lg.l: (In an angry tone) I find you cannot credit me.
I know you take me for an errant ass,
An ass that may be soothed into belief,
And then be used at pleasure.
But, madam, I have been so often cheated
By perjured, soft, deluding hypocrites,
That I’ve no faith left for the cozening sex,
Especially for women of your trade.
The low esteem you have of me, perhaps
May bring my heart again,
For I have pride that yet surmounts my love.

div2.stage: She turns with pride, he holds her

lg.l: Throw off this pride, this enemy to bliss,
And show the power of love: ’tis with those arms
I can be only vanquished, made a slave.
Is all my mighty expectation vanished?
No, I will not hear thee talk, thou hast a charm
In every word, that draws my heart away.
And all the thousand trophies I designed
Thou hast undone. Why art thou soft?
Thy looks are bravely rough, and meant for war.
Could thou not storm on still?
I then perhaps had been as free as thou.

l.seg: Death! how she throws her fire about my soul!

lg.l: Take heed, fair creature, how you raise my hopes,
Which once assumed pretend to all dominion.
There’s not a joy thou hast in store
I shall not then command:
For which I’ll pay thee back my soul, my life.
Come, let’s begin th’account this happy minute.
And will you pay me then the price I ask?
Oh, why dost thou draw me from an awful worship,
By showing thou art no divinity?
Conceal the fiend, and show me all the angel;
Keep me but ignorant, and I’ll be devout,
And pay my vows forever at this shrine.
The pay I mean is but thy love for mine.
Can you give that?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Entirely! Come, let’s withdraw: where I’ll renew my vows, and breathe ’em with such ardor thou shall not doubt my zeal.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Thou hast a power too strong to be resisted.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Now my curse go with you! Is all our project fallen to this? To love the only enemy to our trade? Nay, to love such a shameroon, a very beggar – nay, a pirate-beggar, whose business is to rifle and be gone – a no-purchase, no-pay tatterdemalion, an English piccaroon; a rogue that fights for daily drink and takes a pride in being loyally lousy? Oh, I could curse now, if I durst! This is the fate of most whores:

lg.l: Trophies, which from believing fops we win,
Are spoils to those who cozen us again.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Enter Florinda, Valeria, Hellena, in antic different dresses from what they were in before, Callis attending

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I wonder what should make my brother in so ill a humor: I hope he has not found out our ramble this morning.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: No; if he had, we should have heard on’t at both ears, and have been mewed up this afternoon, which I would not for the world should have happened. Hey ho! I’m sad as a lover’s lute.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Well, methinks we have learnt this trade of gypsies as readily as if we had been bred upon the road to Loretto: and yet I did so fumble when I told the stranger his fortune, that I was afraid I should have told my own and yours by mistake. But methinks Hellena has been very serious ever since.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I would give my garters she were in love, to be revenged upon her, for abusing me. How is’t, Hellena?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Ah, would I had never seen my mad monsieur! And yet for all your laughing I am not in love – and yet this small acquaintance, o my conscience, will never out of my head.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! I laugh to think how thou art fitted with a lover, a fellow that, I warrant, loves every new face he sees.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Hum – He has not kept his word with me here – and may be taken up – that thought is not very pleasant to me – What the deuce should this be now that I feel?

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: What is’t like?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Nay, the lord knows. But if I should be hanged, I cannot choose but be angry and afraid when I think that mad fellow should be in love with anybody but me. What to think of myself I know not; would I could meet with some true damned gypsy, that I might know my fortune.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Know it! Why there’s nothing so easy: thou wilt love this wandering inconstant till thou findst thyself hanged about his neck, and then be as mad to get free again.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Yes, Valeria, we shall see her bestride his baggage horse, and follow him to the campaign.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: So, so, now you are provided for, there’s no care taken of poor me! But since you have set my heart a-wishing, I am resolved to know for what. I will not die of the pip, so I will not.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Art thou mad to talk so? Who will like thee well enough to have thee, that hears what a mad wench thou art?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Like me! I don’t intend every he that likes me shall have me, but he that I like: I should have stayed in the nunnery still if I had liked my lady abbess as well as she liked me. No, I came thence, not (as my wise brother imagines) to take an eternal farewell of the world, but to love and to be beloved; and I will be beloved or I’ll get one of your men, so I will.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Am I put into the number of lovers?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: You! my coz, I know thou art too good-natured to leave us in any design. Thou would venture a cast, though thou comest off a loser, especially with such a gamester. I observed your man, and your willing ears incline that way; and if you are not a lover, ’tis an art soon learnt – (Sighs) that I find.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I wonder how you learnt to love so easily. I had a thousand charms to meet my eyes and ears, ere I could yield; and ’twas the knowledge of Belvile’s merit, not the surprising person, took my soul. Thou art too rash to give a heart at first sight.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Hang your considering lover! I ne’er thought beyond the fancy, that ’twas a very pretty, idle, silly kind of pleasure to pass ones time with, to write little, soft, nonsensical billets and with great difficulty and danger receive answers, in which I shall have my beauty praised, my wit admired (though little or none) and have the vanity and power to know I am desirable; then I have the more inclination that way, because I am to be a nun, and so shall not be suspected to have any such earthly thoughts about me. But when I walk thus, and sigh thus, they’ll think my mind’s upon my monastery, and cry, “how happy ’tis she’s so resolv’d!”. But not a word of man.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: What a mad creature’s this!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I’ll warrant, if my brother hears either of you sigh, he cries (gravely) “I fear you have the indiscretion to be in love, but take heed of the honour of our house and your own unspotted fame”. And so he conjures on till he has laid the soft-winged god in your hearts, or broke the bird’s nest. But see here comes your lover: but where’s my inconstant? let’s step aside, and we may learn something.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What means this? the picture’s taken in.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: It may be the wench is good natured, and will be kind gratis. Your friend’s a proper handsome fellow.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I rather think she has cut his throat and is fled: I am mad he should throw himself into dangers. Pox on’t, I shall want him tonight! Let’s knock and ask for him.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: My heart goes a-pit a-pat, for fear ’tis my man they talk of.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: What would you have?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Tell the stranger that entered here about two hours ago, that his friends stay here for him.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: A curse upon him for Moretta, would he were at the devil! But he’s coming to you.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Aye, aye, ’tis he! Oh, how this vexes me.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: And how, and how, dear lad, has fortune smiled? Are we to break her windows, or raise up altars to her? Hah!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Does not my fortune sit triumphant on my brow? Dost not see the little wanton god there all gay and smiling? Have I not an air about my face and eyes that distinguish me from the crowd of common lovers? By heaven, Cupid’s quiver has not half so many darts as her eyes! Oh such a bona roba , to sleep in her arms is lying in fresco , all perfumed air about me.

p.seg: Here’s fine encouragement for me to fool on.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Hark ye, where didst thou purchase that rich canary we drank today? Tell me, that I may adore the spigot, and sacrifice to the butt: the juice was divine, into which I must dip my rosary and then bless all things that I would have bold or fortunate.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Well, Sir, let’s go take a bottle, and hear the story of your success.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Would not French wine do better?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Damn the hungry balderdash! Cheerful sack has a generous virtue in’t, inspiring a successful confidence, gives eloquence to the tongue and vigor to the soul, and has in a few hours completed all my hopes and wishes. There’s nothing left to raise a new desire in me. Come, let’s be gay and wanton; and, gentlemen, study, study what you want, for here are friends – that will supply, gentlemen – Hark! What a charming sound they make, ’tis he and she gold whilst here, shall beget new pleasures every moment.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: But hark ye, sir, you are not married, are you?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: All the honey of matrimony, but none of the sting, friend.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, thou’rt a fortunate rogue.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I am so, sir, let these inform you. Ha, how sweetly they chime! Pox of poverty, it makes a man a slave, makes wit and honor sneak, my soul grew lean and rusty for want of credit.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Sheartlikins, this I like well, it looks like my lucky bargain! Oh how I long for the approach of my squire that is to conduct me to her house again. Why, here’s two provided for!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: By this light y’re happy men.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Fortune is pleased to smile on us, gentlemen, to smile on us.

div2.stage: Enter Sancho and pulls Blunt by the sleeve; they go aside

sp.speaker: SANCHO
sp.p: Sir, my lady expects you; she has removed all that might oppose your will and pleasure, and is impatient till you come.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Sir, I’ll attend you. Oh the happiest rogue! I’ll take no leave, lest they either dog me, or stay me.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: But then the little gypsy is forgot?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A mischief on thee for putting her into my thoughts! I had quite forgot her else, and this night’s debauch had drunk her quite down.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Had it so, good captain?

p.seg: Ha! I hope she did not hear.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: What, afraid of such a champion?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh, you’re a fine lady of your word, are you not? To make a man languish a whole day –

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: In tedious search of me.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, child, thou’rt in the right, hadst thou seen what a melancholy dog I have been ever since I was a lover, how I have walked the streets like a Capuchin, with my hands in my sleeves – Faith, sweetheart, thou wouldst pity me.

p.seg: Now, if I should be hanged, I can’t be angry with him, he dissembles so heartily.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Poor soul! That’s kindly said, I see thou bearest a conscience. Come then, for a beginning show me thy dear face.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I’m afraid, my small acquaintance, you have been staying that swinging stomach you boasted of this morning: I remember then my little collation would have gone down with you without the sauce of a handsome face. Is your stomach so queasy now?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, long fasting, child, spoils a man’s appetite. Yet if you durst treat, I could so lay about me still.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And would you fall to, before a priest says grace?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh fie, fie, what an old out-of-fashioned thing hast thou named! Thou couldst not dash me more out of countenance shouldst thou show me an ugly face.

div2.stage: Whilst he is seemingly courting Hellena, enter Angellica, Moretta, Biskey, and Sebastian, all in masquerade; Angellica sees Willmore and starts

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Heavens, is’t he? And passionately fond to see another woman?

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: What could you expect less from such a swaggerer?

lg.l: Expect! as much as I paid him: a heart entire,
Which I had pride enough to think when’er I gave
It would have raised the man above the vulgar,
Made him all soul, and that all soft and constant.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: You see, captain, how willing I am to be friends with you, till time and ill-luck make us lovers, and ask you the question first rather than put your modesty to the blush by asking me; for alas, I know you captains are such strict men, severe observers of your vows to chastity, that ’twill be hard to prevail with your tender conscience to marry a young willing maid.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Do not abuse me, for fear I should take thee at thy word and marry thee indeed, which I’m sure will be revenge sufficient.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: O’ my conscience, that will be our destiny, because we are both of one humor: I am as inconstant as you, for I have considered, captain, that a handsome woman has a great deal to do whilst her face is good, for then is our harvest-time to gather friends; and should I in these days of my youth catch a fit of foolish constancy I were undone, ’tis loitering by daylight in our great journey. Therefore declare, I’ll allow but one year for love, one year for indifference, and one year for hate, and then – go hang yourself – for I profess myself the gay, the kind, and the inconstant; the devil’s in’t if this won’t please you.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh most damnably! I have a heart with a hole quite through it too, no prison like mine to keep a mistress in.

p.seg: Perjured man! How I believe thee now!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Well, I see our business as well as humors are alike, yours to cozen as many maids as will trust you, and I as many men as have faith. See if I have not as desperate a lying look, as you can have for the heart of you. (Pulls off her vizard; he starts) How do you like it, captain?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Like it! By Heaven, I never saw so much beauty. Oh, the charms of those sprightly black eyes, that strangely fair face, full of smiles and dimples! Those soft round melting cherry lips! And small even white teeth! Not to be expressed, but silently adored! Oh, one look more, and strike me dumb, or I shall repeat nothing else till I am mad.

div2.stage: He seems to court her to pull off her vizard: she refuses

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I can endure no more! Nor is it fit to interrupt him, for if I do my jealousy has so destroyed my reason – I shall undo him – Therefore I’ll retire. And you Sebastian, (To one of her bravos) follow that woman, and learn who ’tis, (To the other bravo) while you tell the fugitive, I would speak to him instantly.

div2.stage: This while Florinda is talking to Belvile, who stands sullenly, Frederick courting Valeria

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Prithee, dear stranger, be not so sullen, for though you have lost your love you see my friend frankly offers you hers to play with in the meantime.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Faith, madam, I am sorry I can’t play at her game.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Pray leave your intercession, and mind your own affair, they’ll better agree apart: he’s a model sigher in company, but alone no woman escapes him.

p.seg: Sure he does but rally – yet if it should be true – I’ll tempt him farther.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Madam, why am I chose out of all mankind to be the object of your bounty?

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: There’s another civil question asked.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Pox of’s modesty, it spoils his own markets and hinders mine.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, from my window I have often seen you, and women of quality have so few opportunities for love that we ought to lose none.

p.seg: (Take the jewel, fool.)

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: You tempt me strangely, madam, every way.

p.seg: So, if I find him false, my whole repose is gone.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: And but for a vow I’ve made to a very fine lady, this goodness had subdued me.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Pox on’t, be kind, in pity to me be kind, for I am to thrive here but as you treat her friend.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Tell me what did you in yonder house, and I’ll unmask.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Yonder house – oh – I went to – a – to – why, there’s a friend of mine lives there.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: What a she , or a he friend?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A man, upon my honor! A man – “a she friend”! No, no, madam, you have done my business, I thank you.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And was’t your man friend that had more darts in’s eyes than Cupid carries in a whole budget of arrows?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: So –

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Ah, such a bona roba , to be in her arms is lying in fresco , all perfumed air about me – – was this your man friend too?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: So –

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: That gave you the he and the she gold that begets young pleasures?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Well, well, madam, then you see there are ladies in the world that will not be cruel – there are, madam, there are –

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And there be men too as fine, wild, inconstant fellows as yourself, there be, captain, there be, if you go to that now – therefore I’m resolved –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: – to see your face no more –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: – till tomorrow.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, you frighted me.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Nor then neither, unless you’ll swear never to see that lady more.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: See her! Why, never to think of womankind again!

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Kneel, and swear.

div2.stage: Kneels, she gives him her hand

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I do, never to think, to see, to love, nor lie with any but thyself.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Kiss the book.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh, most religiously.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Now what a wicked creature am I, to damn a proper fellow.

sp.speaker: CALLIS
sp.p: (To Florinda) Madam, I’ll stay no longer, ’tis e’en dark.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: However, sir, I’ll leave this with you, that when I’m gone you may repent the opportunity you have lost by your modesty.

div2.stage: Gives him the jewel, which is her picture, and exits; he gazes after her

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: To Hellena ’Twill be an age till tomorrow, and till then I will most impatiently expect you. Adieu, my dear pretty angel.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ha! Florinda’s picture! ’Twas she herself! What a dull dog was I? I would have given the world for one minute’s discourse with her.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: This comes of your modesty, ah pox on your vow, ’twas ten to one but we had lost the jewel by’t.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Willmore! The blessed’st opportunity lost! Florinda, friends, Florinda!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ah rogue! Such black eyes, such a face, such a mouth, such teeth – and so much wit!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: All, all, and a thousand charms besides.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Why, dost thou know her?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Know her! Ay, ay, and a pox take me with all my heart for being modest.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: But hark ye, friend of mine, are you my rival? And have I been only beating the bush all this while?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I understand thee not – I’m mad – see here –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ha! Whose picture is this? ’Tis a fine wench.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: The colonel’s mistress, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Oh, oh, here! (Gives the picture back) I thought it had been another prize! Come, come, a bottle will set thee right again.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I am content to try, and by that time ’twill be late enough for our design.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Agreed.

lg.l: Love does all day the soul’s great empire keep,
But wine at night lulls the soft god asleep.

div2.head: SCENE 2
div2.stage: Enter Blunt and Lucetta with a light

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: Now we are safe and free, no fears of the coming home of my old jealous husband, which made me a little thoughtful when you came in first; but now love is all the business of my soul.

p.seg: I am transported – pox on’t, that I had but some fine things to say to her, such as lovers use – I was a fool not to learn of Fred a little by heart before I came – something I must say.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: I have nothing to pay for so great a favor, but such a love as cannot but be great since at first sight of that sweet face and shape it made me your absolute captive.

p.seg: Kind heart, how prettily she talks! Egad, I’ll show her husband a Spanish trick: send him out of the world and marry her. She’s damnably in love with me, and will ne’er mind settlements, and so there’s that said.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
