sp.p: Well, Sir, I’ll go and undress me, and be with you instantly.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Make haste then, for ’dsheartlikins, dear soul, thou canst not guess at the pain of a longing lover when his joys are drawn within the compass of a few minutes.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: You speak my sense, and I’ll make haste to provide it.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Tis a rare girl, and this one night’s enjoyment with her will be worth all the days I ever passed in Essex. Would she’d go with me into England, though to say truth there’s plenty of whores there already. But a pox on ’em, they are such mercenary prodigal whores that they want such a one as this, that’s free and generous, to give ’em good examples. Why, what a house she has! How rich and fine!

sp.speaker: SANCHO
sp.p: Sir, my lady has sent me to conduct you to her chamber.

p.seg: Here’s one of her servants too: ’dsheartlikins, by his garb and gravity he might be a justice of peace in Essex, and is but a pimp here.

div2.stage: The scene changes to a chamber with an alcove bed in it, a table, etc. Lucetta in bed; enter Sancho and Blunt, who takes the candle of Sancho at the door

sp.speaker: SANCHO
sp.p: Sir, my commission reaches no farther.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Sir, I’ll excuse your complement. What, in bed, my sweet mistress?

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: You see, I still outdo you in kindness.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: And thou shall see what haste I’ll make to quit scores. Oh, the luckiest rogue!

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: Should you be false or cruel now!

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: False, ’sheartlikins, what dost thou take me for, a Jew? An insensible heathen? A pox of thy old jealous husband; and he were dead, egad, sweet soul, it should be none of my fault if I did not marry thee.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: It never should be mine.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Good soul, I’m the fortunatest dog!

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: Are you not undressed yet?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: As much as my impatience will permit.

div2.stage: Goes towards the bed in his shirt and drawers

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: Hold, sir, put out the light, it may betray us else.

p.seg: ’Sheartlikins, there I think I had it.

div2.stage: Enter Lucetta, Philippo, and Sancho with a light

sp.speaker: PHILIPPO
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, he’s dispatched finely.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: Now, sir, had I been coy, we had missed of this booty.

sp.speaker: PHILIPPO
sp.p: Nay, when I saw ’twas a substantial fool I was mollified; but when you dote upon a serenading coxcomb, upon a face, fine clothes, and a lute, it makes me rage.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: You know I never was guilty of that folly, my dear Philippo, but with yourself. But come, let’s see what we have got by this.

sp.speaker: PHILIPPO
sp.p: A rich coat! Sword and hat! These breeches too are well-lined! See here, a gold watch! A purse, ha! Gold, at least two hundred pistoles! A bunch of diamond rings, and one with the family arms! A gold box, with a medal of his king! And his lady mother’s picture! These were sacred reliques, believe me! See, the waistband of his breeches have a mine of gold! Old queen Bess’s: we have a quarrel to her ever since eighty-eight, and may therefore justify the theft, the Inquisition might have committed it.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: See, a bracelet of bowed gold, these his sister tied about his arm at parting. But well, for all this I fear his being a stranger may make a noise, and hinder our trade with them hereafter.

sp.speaker: PHILIPPO
sp.p: That’s our security: he is not only a stranger to us, but to the country too. The common sewer into which he is descended, thou knowst, conducts him into another street, which this light will hinder him from ever finding again. He knows neither your name, nor the street where your house is, nay, nor the way to his own lodgings.

sp.speaker: LUCETTA
sp.p: And art not thou an unmerciful rogue, not to afford him one night for all this? I should not have been such a Jew.

sp.speaker: PHILIPPO
sp.p: Blame me not, Lucetta, to keep as much of thee as I can to myself. Come, that thought makes me wanton, let’s to bed. Sancho, lock up these.

lg.l: This is the fleece which fools do bear,
Designed for witty men to sheer.

div2.stage: The scene changes, and discovers blunt creeping out of a common sewer, his face, etc. all dirty

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Oh lord! (Climbing up) I am got out at last, and (which is a miracle) without a clue! And now to damning and cursing; but if that would ease me, where shall I begin? With my fortune, myself, or the queen that cozened me – what a dog was I to believe in women! Oh coxcomb! Ignorant conceited coxcomb! To fancy she could be enamored with my person, at the first sight enamored – oh, I’m a cursed puppy, ’tis plain: fool was writ upon my forehead, she perceived it, saw the Essex calf there – for what allurements could there be in this countenance, which I can endure because I’m acquainted with it? Oh, dull silly dog! To be thus soothed into a cozening! Had I been drunk, I might fondly have credited the young queen! But as I was in my right wits, to be thus cheated confirms I am a dull believing English country fop. But my comrades! Death and the devil, there’s the worst of all! Then a ballad will be sung tomorrow on the Prado , to a lousy tune of the enchanted squire and the annihilated damsel. But Fred, that rogue, and the colonel will abuse me beyond all Christian patience. Had she left me my clothes I have a bill of exchange at home would have saved my credit. But now all hope is taken from me. Well, I’ll home (if I can find the way) with this consolation: that I am not the first kind believing coxcomb; but there are, gallants, many such good natures amongst ye.

lg.l: And tho you’ve better arts to hide your follies,
Adsheartlikins y’are all as errant cullies.

div2.head: SCENE 3
div2.stage: Enter Florinda undressed, with a key and a little box

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Well, thus far I’m in my way to happiness: I have got myself free from Callis; my brother too, I find by yonder light, is gone into his cabinet, and thinks not of me; I have by good fortune got the key of the garden backdoor, I’ll open it to prevent Belvile’s knocking, a little noise will now alarm my brother. Now am I as fearful as a young thief. (Unlocks the door) Hark, what noise is that? Oh,’twas the wind that played amongst the boughs. Belvile stays long, methinks it’s time – stay – for fear of a surprise, I’ll hide these jewels in yonder jasmine.

div2.stage: She goes to lay down the box

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What the devil is become of these fellows, Belvile and Frederick? They promised to stay at the next corner for me, but who the devil knows the corner of a full moon? Now, whereabouts am I? Hah, what have we here? A garden! A very convenient place to sleep in! Hah, what has God sent us here? A female – by this light, a woman! I’m a dog if it be not a very wench.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: He’s come! Hah, who’s there?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Sweet soul, let me salute thy shoestring.

p.seg: ’Tis not my Belvile; good heavens, I know him not.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Prithee, prithee, child, not so many hard questions; let it suffice I am here, child. Come, come kiss me.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Good gods! What luck is mine?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Only good luck, child, parlous good luck, come hither. ’Tis a delicate shining wench, by this hand she’s perfumed and smells like any nosegay. Prithee, dear soul, let’s not play the fool and lose time, precious time, for as God shall save me I’m as honest a fellow as breathes, though I am a little disguised at present. Come, I say, why, thou mayest be free with me, I’ll be very secret. I’ll not boast who ’twas obliged me, not I, for hang me if I know thy name.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Heavens! What a filthy beast is this!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I am so, and thou oughtst the sooner to lie with me for that reason, for look you, child, there will be no sin in’t, because ’twas neither designed nor premeditated; ’tis pure accident on both sides – that’s a certain thing now. Indeed, should I make love to you, and you vow fidelity and swear and lie till you believed and yielded, thou art therefore (as thou art a good Christian) obliged in conscience to deny me nothing. Now come, be kind, without any more idle prating.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Oh, I am ruined! Wicked man, unhand me!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Wicked! Egad, child, a judge, were he young and vigorous and saw those eyes of thine, would know ’twas they gave the first blow, the first provocation.Come, prithee let’s lose no time, I say, this is a fine convenient place.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, let me go, I conjure you, or I’ll call out!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ay, ay, you were best to call witness to see how finely you treat me, do.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I’ll cry murder, rape, or anything, if you do not instantly let me go!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A rape! Come, come, you lie, you baggage, you lie. What, I’ll warrant you would fain have the world believe now that you are not so forward as I. No, not you, why at this time of night was your cobweb-door set open, dear spider, but to catch flies? Hah, come, or I shall be damnably angry. Why, what a coil is here.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, can you think –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: That you’d do it for nothing? Oh, oh, I find what you’d be at. Look here, here’s a pistole for you; here’s a work indeed, here, take it, I say.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: For Heaven’s sake, sir, as you’re a gentleman –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: So, now, she would be wheedling me for more. What, you will not take it then? You’re resolved you will not. Come, come, take it, or I’ll put it up again; for, look ye, I never give more. Why, how now, mistress, are you so high i’th’ mouth a pistole won’t down with you? Hah, why, what a work’s here – in good time – come, no struggling, be gone – but an y’are good at a dumb wrestle, I’m for ye – look ye – I’m for ye

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: The door is open, a pox of this mad fellow, I’m angry that we’ve lost him, I durst have sworn he had followed us.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: But you were so hasty, colonel, to be gone.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Help, help, murder! Help! Oh, I’m ruined!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ha, sure that’s Florinda’s voice! (Comes up to them) A man! Villain, let go that lady!

div2.stage: Willmore turns and draws, Frederick interposes

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Belvile! Heavens! My brother too is coming, and ’twill be impossible to escape. Belvile, I conjure you to walk under my chamber window, from whence I’ll give you some instructions what to do; This rude man has undone us!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Belvile!

div2.stage: Enter Pedro, Stephano, and other servants with lights

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I’m betrayed! Run, Stephano, and see if Florinda be safe. Exit Stephano So whoe’er they be, all is not well, I’ll to Florinda’s chamber.

div2.stage: They fight, and Pedro’s party beats ’em out; going out, meets Stephano

sp.speaker: STEPHANO
sp.p: You need not, sir, the poor lady’s fast asleep, and thinks no harm. I would not wake her, sir, for fear of frightening her with your danger.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I’m glad she’s there. Rascals, how came the garden door open?

sp.speaker: STEPHANO
sp.p: That question comes too late, sir: some of my fellow servants masquerading, I’ll warrant.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Masquerading! a lewd custom to debauch our youth; there’s something more in this than I imagine.

div2.head: SCENE 4
div2.stage: Enter Belvile in rage, Frederick holding him, and Willmore melancholy

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Why, how the devil should I know Florinda?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ah plague of your ignorance! If it had not been Florinda, must you be a beast? A brute, a senseless swine?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Well, sir, you see I am endued with patience, I can bear, though egad y’re very free with me methinks, I was in good hopes the quarrel would have been on my side for so uncivilly interrupting me.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Peace, brute, whilst thou’rt safe – oh, I’m distracted.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, nay, I’m an unlucky dog, that’s certain.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ah curse upon the star that ruled my birth! Or whatsoever other influence that makes me still so wretched.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Thou break’st my heart with these complaints: there is no star in fault, no influence but sack, the cursed sack I drank.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Why, how the devil came you so drunk?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Why, how the devil came you so sober?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: A curse upon his thin skull, he was always beforehand that way.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Prithee, dear colonel, forgive him, he’s sorry for his fault.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: He’s always so after he has done a mischief. A plague on all such brutes.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: By this light I took her for an errant harlot.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Damn your debauched opinion; tell me, sot, hadst thou so much sense and light about thee to distinguish her to be a woman, and couldst not see something about her face and person to strike an awful reverence into thy soul?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith no, I considered her as mere a woman as I could wish.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: ’Sdeath I have no patience: draw, or I’ll kill you.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Let that alone till tomorrow, and if I set not all right again use your pleasure.

lg.l: Tomorrow, damn it.
The spiteful light will lead me to no happiness.
Tomorrow is Antonio’s, and perhaps
Guides him to my undoing; oh, that I could meet
This rival, this powerful fortunate.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Let thy own reason, or my rage instruct thee.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I shall be finely informed then, no doubt; hear me, colonel – hear me – show me the man and I’ll do his business.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I know him no more than thou, or if I did I should not need thy aid.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: This you say is Angellica’s House, I promised the kind baggage to lie with her to night.

div2.stage: Enter Antonio and his page Diego ; Antonio knocks on the hilt of his sword

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: You paid the thousand crowns I directed?

sp.speaker: DIEGO
sp.p: To the lady’s old woman, sir, I did.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Who the devil have we here?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I’ll now plant myself under Florinda’s window, and if I find no comfort there, I’ll die.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Page!

sp.speaker: DIEGO
sp.p: Here’s my lord.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How is this, a picaroon going to board my frigate! Here’s one chase gun for you

div2.stage: Drawing his sword, justles Antonio who turns and draws; they fight, Antonio falls

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: Oh, bless us, we are all undone!

div2.stage: Runs in, and shuts the door

sp.speaker: DIEGO
sp.p: Help, murder!

div2.stage: Belvile returns at the noise of fighting

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ha, the mad rogue’s engaged in some unlucky adventure again.

sp.speaker: MASQUERADER
sp.p: Ha, a man killed!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: How, a man killed! Then I’ll go home to sleep.

div2.stage: Puts up, and reels out; exit maskers another way

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Who should it be? Pray Heaven the rogue is safe, for all my quarrel to him.

div2.stage: As Belvile is groping about, enter an officer and six soldiers

sp.speaker: SOLDIER
sp.p: Who’s there?

sp.speaker: OFFICER
sp.p: So, here’s one dispatched! Secure the murderer.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Do not mistake my charity for murder: I came to his assistance.

sp.speaker: OFFICER
sp.p: That shall be tried, sir. St. Jago, swords drawn in the carnival time!

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Thy hand prithee.

sp.speaker: OFFICER
sp.p: Ha, Don Antonio! Look well to the villain there. How is’t, sir?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’m hurt.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Has my humanity made me a criminal?

sp.speaker: OFFICER
sp.p: Away with him.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What a cursed chance is this!

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (To the officer) This is the man that has set upon me twice; carry him to my apartment till you have further orders from me.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Discovers Belvile, as by dark alone

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: When shall I be weary of railing on fortune, who is resolved never to turn with smiles upon me? Two such defeats in one night, none but the devil and that mad rogue could have contrived to have plagued me with. I am here a prisoner, but where? Heaven knows! And if there be murder done, I can soon decide the fate of a stranger in a nation without mercy. Yet this is nothing to the torture my soul bows with when I think of losing my fair, my dear Florinda. Hark, my door opens! A light – a man – and seems of quality – armed too. Now shall I die like a dog without defense.

div2.stage: Enter Antonio in a night gown with a light, his arm in a scarf and a sword under his arm; he sets the candle on the table

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Sir, I come to know what injuries I have done you that could provoke you to so mean an action as to attack me basely, without allowing time for my defense.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Sir, for a man in my circumstances to plead innocence, would look like fear; but view me well, and you will find no marks of a coward on me, nor any thing that betrays that brutality you accuse me of.

lg.l: In vain, sir, you impose upon my sense,
You are not only he who drew on me last night,
But yesterday before the same house, that of Angellica.
Yet there is something in your face and mien –

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I own I fought today in the defense of a friend of mine, with whom you (if you’re the same) and your party were first engaged.

lg.l: Perhaps you think this crime enough to kill me,
But if you do, I cannot fear you’ll do it basely.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: No, Sir, I’ll make you fit for a defense with this.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: This gallantry surprises me, nor know I how to use this present, sir, against a man so brave.

lg.l: You shall not need,
For know I come to snatch you from a danger
That is decreed against you:
Perhaps your life, or long imprisonment,
And ’twas with so much courage you offended,
I cannot see you punished.
How shall I pay this generosity?
It had been safer to have killed another,
Than have attempted me:
To show your danger, sir, I’ll let you know my quality:
And ’tis the viceroy’s son whom you have wounded.

l.seg: The viceroy’s son!
Death and confusion! Was this plague reserved
To complete all the rest? Obliged by him!
The man of all the world I would destroy.

lg.l: You seem disordered, sir.
Yes, trust me, sir, I am, and ’tis with pain
That man receives such bounties,
Who wants the power to pay ’em back again.
To gallant spirits ’tis indeed uneasy;
But you may quickly overpay me, sir.

l.seg: Then I am well, kind Heaven! But set us even,
That I may fight with him and keep my honor safe.

lg.l: Oh, I’m impatient, sir, to be discounting
The mighty debt I owe you: command me quickly –
I have a quarrel with a rival, sir,
About the maid we love.

l.seg: Death, ’tis Florinda he means!
That thought destroys my reason, and I shall kill him.

lg.l: My rival, sir,
Is one has all the virtues man can boast of.

l.seg: Death! Who should this be?

lg.l: He challenged me to meet him on the Molo,
As soon as day appeared; but last night’s quarrel
Has made my arm unfit to guide a sword.
I apprehend you, Sir, you’d have me kill the man
That lays a claim to the maid you speak of.
I’ll do’t, I’ll fly to do it.
Sir, do you know her?
No, sir, but ’tis enough she is admired by you.
Sir, I shall rob you of the glory on’t,
For you must fight under my name and dress.
That opinion must be strangely obliging that makes
You think I can personate the brave Antonio,
Whom I can but strive to imitate.
You say too much to my advantage.
Come, sir, the day appears that calls you forth.
Within, sir, is the habit.
Fantastic fortune, thou deceitful light,
That cheats the wearied traveler by night,
Though on a precipice each step you tread,
I am resolved to follow where you lead.

div2.head: SCENE 2
div2.stage: Enter Florinda and Callis in masks, with Stephano

l.seg: I’m dying with my fears; Belvile’s not coming,
As I expected, underneath my window,
Makes me believe that all those fears are true.

lg.l: Canst thou not tell with whom my brother fights?

sp.speaker: STEPHANO
sp.p: No, Madam, they were both in masquerade; I was by when they challenged one another and they had decided the quarrel then, but were prevented by some cavaliers, which made ’em put it off till now; but I am sure ’tis about you they fight.

p.seg: Nay then ’tis with Belvile, for what other lover have I that dares fight for me, except Antonio? And he is too much in favor with my brother. If it be he, for whom shall I direct my prayers to Heaven?

sp.speaker: STEPHANO
sp.p: Madam, I must leave you, for if my master see me I shall be hanged for being your conductor. I escaped narrowly for the excuse I made for you last night i’th’ garden.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: And I’ll reward thee for’t, prithee no more.

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro in his masking habit

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Antonio’s late today, the place will fill, and we may be prevented.

p.seg: Antonio! Sure I heard amiss.

lg.l: But who would not excuse a happy lover,
When soft fair arms confine the yielding neck,
And the kind whisper languishingly breathes,
Must you be gone so soon?
Sure I had dwelt for ever on her bosom.
But stay, he’s here.

div2.stage: Enter Belvile dressed in Antonio’s clothes

p.seg: ’Tis not Belvile, half my fears are vanished!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Antonio!

p.seg: This must be he.

lg.l: The wretched, sir, are watchful, and ’tis enough
You have the advantage of me in Angellica.

l.seg: Angellica!
Or I’ve mistook my man, Or else Antonio,
Can he forget his interest in Florinda
And fight for common prize?

lg.l: Come, sir, you know our terms.

l.seg: By Heaven, not I.

div2.stage: Offers to fight; Florinda runs in

lg.l: (To Belvile) Oh, hold! Whoe’er you be, I do conjure you hold!
If you strike here, I die.
Florinda!

l.seg: Florinda imploring for my rival!

lg.l: Away, this kindness is unseasonable.

div2.stage: Puts her by, they fight; she runs in just as Belvile disarms Pedro

lg.l: Who are you, sir, that dare deny my prayers?
Thy prayers destroy him, if thou wouldst preserve him.
Do that thou’rt unacquainted with, and curse him.
By all you hold most dear, by her you love,
I do conjure you, touch him not.
By her I love!
See, I obey, and at your feet resign
The useless trophy of my victory.

div2.stage: Lays his sword at her feet

lg.l: Antonio, you’ve done enough to prove you love Florinda.
Love Florinda!
Does Heaven love adoration, prayer, or penitence?
Love her! Here, sir, your sword again.
lg.stage: (Snatches up the sword, and gives it him)
lg.l: Upon this truth I’ll fight my life away.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: No, you’ve redeemed my sister, and my friendship.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Don Pedro!

div2.stage: He gives him Florinda and pulls off his vizard to show his face, and puts it on again

lg.l: Can you resign your claims to other women,
And give your heart entirely to Florinda?
Entire, as dying saints confessions are.
I can delay my happiness no longer:
This minute let me make Florinda mine.
This minute let it be, no time so proper,
This night my father will arrive from Rome,
And possibly may hinder what we propose.

p.seg: Oh heavens! This minute!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Oh, do not ruin me!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: The place begins to fill; and that we may not be observed, do you walk off to St. Peter’s church where I will meet you and conclude your happiness?

p.seg: if there be no more saints’ churches in Naples.

lg.l: Oh stay, sir, and recall your hasty doom:
Alas, I have not yet prepared my heart
To entertain so strange a guest.
Away, this silly modesty is assumed too late.
Heaven, madam! What do you do?
Do? Despise the man that lays a tyrant’s claim
To what he ought to conquer by submission!
You do not know me; move a little this way.
Yes, you may even force me to the altar,
But not the holy man that offers there
Shall force me to be thine.

div2.stage: Pedro talks to Callis this while

lg.l: Oh, do not lose so blessed an opportunity!
See, ’tis your Belvile, not Antonio,
Whom your mistaken scorn and anger ruins.
Belvile!
Where was my soul it could not meet thy voice,
And take this knowledge in?

div2.stage: As they are talking, enter Willmore finely dressed, and Frederick

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: No intelligence! No news of Belvile yet! Well, I am the most unlucky rascal in nature. Ha, am I deceived, or is it he? Look, Fred, ’tis he! My dear Belvile!

div2.stage: Runs and embraces him; Belvile’s vizard falls out on’s hand

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Hell and confusion seize thee!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Ha! Belvile! I beg your pardon, sir.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Nay, touch her not, she’s mine by conquest, sir. I won her by my sword.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Did’st thou so? And egad, child, we’ll keep her by the sword.

div2.stage: Draws on Pedro; Belvile goes between

lg.l: Stand off.
Thou’rt so profanely lewd, so curst by Heaven,
All quarrels thou espousest must be fatal.
Nay, and you be so hot, my valor’s coy,
And shall be courted when you want it next.
(To Pedro) You know I ought to claim a victor’s right,
But you’re the brother to divine Florinda,
To whom I’m such a slave; to purchase her,
I durst not hurt the man she holds so dear.
’Twas by Antonio’s, not by Belvile’s Sword,
This question should have been decided, sir:
I must confess much to your bravery’s due,
Both now, and when I met you last in arms.
But I am nicely punctual in my word,
As men of honor ought, and beg your pardon,
For this mistake another time shall clear.
lg.stage: Aside to Florinda as they are going out

l.seg: This was some plot between you and Belvile,
But I’ll prevent you.

div2.stage: Belvile looks after her, and begins to walk up and down in a rage

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Do not be modest now, and lose the woman; but if we shall fetch her back, so –

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Do not speak to me.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Not speak to you! Egad, I’ll speak to you, and will be answered too.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Will you, sir?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I know I’ve done some mischief, but I’m so dull a puppy that I am the son of a whore, if I know how, or where. Prithee inform my understanding.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Leave me, I say, and leave me instantly.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I will not leave you in this humor, nor till I know my crime.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Death, I’ll tell you, sir –

div2.stage: Draws and runs at Willmore; he runs out, Belvile after him; Frederick interposes

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Ha! Sebastian, is not that Willmore? Haste, haste, and bring him back.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: The colonel’s mad, I never saw him thus before; I’ll after ’em, lest he do some mischief, for I am sure Willmore will not draw on him.

lg.l: I am all rage! my first desires defeated
For one, for ought he knows, that has no
Other merit than her quality,
Her being Don Pedro’s sister, he loves her.
I know ’tis so – dull, dull, insensible –
He will not see me now though oft invited,
And broke his word last night – false perjured man!
He that but yesterday fought for my favors,
And would have made his life a sacrifice
To’ve gained one night with me,
Must now be hired and courted to my arms.

sp.speaker: MORETTA
sp.p: I told you what would come on’t, but Moretta’s an old doating fool. Why did you give him five hundred crowns, but to set himself out for other lovers? You should have kept him poor, if you had meant to have had any good from him.

lg.l: Oh, name not such mean trifles. Had I given him all
My youth has earned from sin,
I had not lost a thought nor sigh upon’t.
But I have given him my eternal rest,
My whole repose, my future joys, my heart,
My virgin heart. Moretta! Oh, ’tis gone!
Curse on him, here he comes;
How fine she has made him too!

div2.stage: Enter Willmore and Sebastian; Angellica turns and walks away]

lg.l: How now, turned shadow?
Fly when I pursue, and follow when I fly!
Stay, gentle shadow of my dove,
And tell me e’er I go,
Whether the substance may not prove
A fleeting thing like you.
There’s a soft kind look remaining yet.

div2.stage: As she turns, she looks on him

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Well, sir, you may be gay, all happiness, all joys pursue you still, fortune’s your slave, and gives you every hour choice of new hearts and beauties till you are cloyed with the repeated bliss which others vainly languish for. But know, false man, that I shall be reveng’d.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: So, ’gad, there are of those faint-hearted lovers, whom such a sharp lesson next their hearts would make as impotent as fourscore. Pox o’ this whining, my business is to laugh and love, a pox on’t. I hate your sullen lover, a man shall lose as much time to put you in humor now as would serve to gain a new woman.

lg.l: I scorn to cool that fire I cannot raise,
Or do the drudgery of your virtuous mistress.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: A virtuous mistress! Death, what a thing thou hast found out for me! Why what the devil should I do with a virtuous woman? A fort of ill-natured creatures, that take a pride to torment a lover. Virtue is but an infirmity in women, a disease that renders even the handsome ungrateful; whilst the ill-favored, for want of solicitations and address, only fancy themselves so. I have lain with a woman of quality who has all the while been railing at qhores.

lg.l: I will not answer for your mistress’s virtue,
Though she be young enough to know no guilt:
And I could wish you would persuade my heart
’Twas the two hundred thousand crowns you courted.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Two hundred thousand crowns! What story’s this? What trick? What woman? Ha.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: How strange you make it! Have you forgot the creature you entertained on the piazza last night?

p.seg: Ha, my gypsy worth two hundred thousand crowns! Oh how I long to be with her! Pox, I knew she was of quality.

lg.l: False man, I see my ruin in thy face.
How many vows you breathed upon my bosom,
Never to be unjust; have you forgot so soon?

p.seg: But here’s a humor indeed would make a man a saint. Would she’d be angry enough to leave me, and command me not to wait on her.

div2.stage: Enter Hellena dressed in man’s clothes

p.seg: This must be Angellica, I know it by her mumping matron here; aye, aye, ’tis she. My mad captain’s with her too, for all his swearing! How this unconstant humor makes me love him!
I hope ’tis one from Don Antonio.
Well, something I’ll do to vex him for this.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I will not speak with him. Am I in humor to receive a lover?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Not speak with him! Why I’ll be gone, and wait your idler minutes. Can I show less obedience to the thing I love so fondly?

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: A fine excuse, this. Stay.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: And hinder your advantage: should I repay your bounties so ungratefully?

lg.l: Come hither, boy, that I may let you see
How much above the advantages you name
I prize one minute’s joy with you.

p.seg: Death, how shall I get away?

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I see you’re impatient; yet you shall stay.

p.seg: And miss my assignation with my gypsy!

div2.stage: Moretta brings Hellena, who addresses herself to Angellica

lg.l: Madam,
You’ll hardly pardon my intrusion
When you shall know my business,
And I’m too young to tell my tale with art,
But there must be a wondrous store of goodness
Where so much beauty dwells.
A pretty advocate, whoever sent thee.
Prithee proceed;
nay, sir, you shall not go.

l.seg: Then shall I lose my dear gypsy forever.
Pox on’t, she stays me out of spite.

lg.l: I am related to a lady, madam,
Young, rich, and nobly born, but has the fate
To be in love with a young English gentleman.
Strangely she loves him, at first sight she loved him,
But did adore him when she heard him speak;
For he, she said, had charms in every word,
That failed not to surprise, to wound, and conquer –

p.seg: Ha, egad I hope this concerns me.

l.seg: ’Tis my false man, he means, would he were gone.
This praise will raise his pride and ruin me.

lg.l: To Willmore Well,
Since you are so impatient to be gone,
I will release you, sir.

p.seg: Nay, then I’m sure ’twas me he spoke of, this cannot be the effects of kindness in her.

lg.l: No, madam, I’ve considered better on’t,
And will not give you cause of jealousy.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: But, sir, I’ve – business, that –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: This shall not do, I know ’tis but to try me.

p.seg: though ’twill undo me.

lg.l: With this addition to his other beauties,
He won her unresisting tender heart,
He vowed and sighed, and swore he loved her dearly;
And she believed the cunning flatterer,
And thought herself the happiest maid alive.
Today was the appointed time by both,
To consummate their bliss;
The virgin, altar, and the priest were dressed,
And whilst she languished for the expected bridegroom,
She heard, he paid his broken vows to you.

p.seg: So, this is some dear rogue that’s in love with me, and this way lets me know it. Or if it be not me, she means someone whose place I may supply.

lg.l: Now I perceive
The cause of thy impatience to be gone,
And all the business of this glorious dress.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Damn the young prater, I know not what he means.

lg.l: Madam,
In your fair eyes I read too much concern
To tell my farther business.
Prithee, sweet youth, talk on, thou mayest perhaps
Raise here a storm that may undo my passion,
And then I’ll grant thee anything.
Madam,’tis to intreat you, (oh unreasonable!)
You would not see this stranger;
For if you do, she vows you are undone,
Though nature never made a man so excellent,
And sure he’ad been a god but for inconstancy.

p.seg: Ah, rogue, how finely he’s instructed! ’Tis plain some woman that has seen me en passant .

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Oh, I shall burst with jealousy! Do you know the man you speak of?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Yes, madam, he used to be in buff and scarlet.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: (To Willmore) Thou, false as Hell, what canst thou say to this?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: By Heaven –

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Hold, do not damn thyself –

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Nor hope to be believed.

lg.l: Oh, perjured man!
Is’t thus you pay my generous passion back?
Why would you, sir, abuse my lady’s faith?
And use me so inhumanly?
A maid so young, so innocent –
Ah, young devil!
Dost thou not know thy life is in my power?
Or think my lady cannot be revenged?

l.seg: So, so, the storm comes finely on.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Now thou art silent, guilt has struck thee dumb.

lg.l: Oh, hadst thou still been so, I’d lived in safety.

p.seg: Sweetheart, the lady’s name and house, quickly: I’m impatient to be with her.

div2.stage: Looks towards Angellica to watch her turning; and as she comes towards them, he meets her

p.seg: So now is he for another woman.

lg.l: The impudent’st young thing in nature!
I cannot persuade him out of his error, madam.
I know he’s in the right, yet thou’st a tongue
That would persuade him to deny his faith.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Said softly to Hellena Her name, her name, dear boy.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Have you forgot it, sir?

p.seg: Oh, I perceive he’s not to know I am a stranger to his lady.

lg.l: Yes, yes, I do know – but – I have forgot the –
By Heaven, such early confidence I never saw.
Did I not charge you with this mistress, sir?
Which you denied, though I beheld your perjury.
This little generosity of thine has rendered back my heart.

l.seg: So, you have made sweet work here, my little mischief;
Look your lady be kind and good-natured now, or
I shall have but a cursed bargain on’t.

lg.l: The rogue’s bred up to bischief,
Art thou so great a fool to credit him?
Yes, I do; and you in vain impose upon me.
Come hither, boy: is not this he you speak of?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: I think – it is. I cannot swear, but I vow he has just such another lying lover’s look.

div2.stage: Hellena looks in his face, he gazes on her

lg.l: Hah! Do not I know that face?

l.seg: By Heaven, my little gypsy! What a dull dog was I!
Had I but looked that way, I’d known her.
Are all my hopes of a new woman banished?

lg.l: Egad, if I don’t fit thee for this, hang me.
Madam, I have found out the plot.

p.seg: Oh Lord, what does he say? Am I discovered now?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Do you see this young spark here?

p.seg: He’ll tell her who I am.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Who do you think this is?

p.seg: Ay, ay, he does know me.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, nay, no cogging; she shall know what a precious mistress I have.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Will you be such a devil?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, nay, I’ll teach you to spoil sport you will not make. This small ambassador comes not from a person of quality, as you imagine and he says, but from a very errant gypsy, the talkingest, pratingest, cantingest little animal thou ever saw’st.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: What news you tell me! That’s the thing I mean.

p.seg: Would I were well off the place, if ever I go a Captain-hunting again.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Mean that thing? That gypsy thing? Thou mayest as well be jealous of thy monkey, or parrot as her; a German motion were worth a dozen of her, and a dream were a better enjoyment, a creature of constitution fitter for Heaven than man.

p.seg: Though I’m sure he lies, yet this vexes me.

lg.l: You are mistaken, she’s a Spanish woman
Made up of no such dull materials.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Materials! Egad, and she be made of any that will either dispense, or admit of love, I’ll be bound to continence.

p.seg: Unreasonable man, do you think so?
You may return, my little brazen head, and tell your lady that till she be handsome enough to be beloved, or I dull enough to be religious, there will be small hopes of me.
Did you not promise then to marry her?
Not I, by Heaven!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: You cannot undeceive my fears and torments, till you have vowed you will not marry her.

p.seg: If he swears that, he’ll be revenged on me indeed for all my rogueries.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I know what arguments you’ll bring against me: fortune and honor.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Honor! I tell you, I hate it in your sex, and those that fancy themselves possessed of that foppery are the most impertinently troublesome of all womankind, and will transgress nine commandments to keep one. And to satisfy your jealousy I swear –

p.seg: Oh, no swearing, dear captain –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: – if it were possible I should ever be inclined to marry, it should be some kind young sinner, one that has generosity enough to give a favor handsomely to one that can ask it discreetly, one that has wit enough to manage an intrigue of love – oh, how civil such a wench is, to a man than does her the honor to marry her!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: By Heaven, there’s no faith in anything he says.

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: Madam, Don Antonio –

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Come hither.

p.seg: Ha, Antonio! He may be coming hither, and he’ll certainly discover me, I’ll therefore retire without a ceremony.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: I’ll see him, get my coach ready.

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: It waits you, madam.

p.seg: (This is lucky.)

lg.l: Dull man, that canst not see how ill, how poor
That false dissimulation looks. Be gone,
And never let me see thy cozening face again,
Lest I relapse and kill thee.

p.seg: Now for my gypsy

lg.l: For though to worse we change, yet still we find
New joys, new charms, in a new miss that’s kind.
He’s gone, and in this ague of my soul
The shivering fit returns;
Oh, with what willing haste he took his leave,
As if the longed for minute were arrived,
Of some blessed assignation.
In vain I have consulted all my charms,
In vain this beauty prized, in vain believed
My eyes could kindle any lasting fires.
I had forgot my name, my infamy,
And the reproach that honor lays on those
That dare pretend a sober passion here.
Nice reputation, though it leave behind
More virtues than inhabit where that dwells,
Yet that once gone, those virtues shine no more.
Then since I am not fit to beloved,
I am resolved to think on a revenge
On him that soothed me thus to my undoing.

div2.head: SCENE 3
div2.stage: Enter Florinda and Valeria in habits different from what they have been seen in

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: We’re happily escaped, yet I tremble still.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: A lover and fear! Why, I am but half a one, and yet I have courage for any attempt. Would Hellena were here! I would fain have had her as deep in this mischief as we, she’ll fare but ill else I doubt.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: She pretended a visit to the Augustine nuns, but I believe some other design carried her out, pray heavens we light on her. Prithee what didst do with Callis?

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: When I saw no reason would do good on her, I followed her into the wardrobe, and as she was looking for something in a great chest I tumbled her in by the heels, snatched the key of the apartment where you were confined, locked her in, and left her bawling for help.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: ’Tis well you resolve to follow my fortunes, for thou darest never appear at home again after such an action.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: That’s according as the young stranger and I shall agree. But to our business: I delivered your letter, your note to Belvile, when I got out under pretense of going to mass, I found him at his lodging and believe me it came seasonably, for never was man in so desperate a condition. I told him of your resolution of making your escape today, if your brother would be absent long enough to permit you; if not, die rather than be Antonio’s.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Thou shouldst have told him I was confined to my chamber upon my brother’s suspicion, that the business on the Molo was a plot laid between him and I.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: I said all this, and told him your brother was now gone to his devotion, and he resolves to visit every church till he find him; and not only undeceive him in that, but caress him so as shall delay his return home.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Oh heavens! he’s here, and Belvile with him too.

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro, Belvile, Willmore; Belvile and Don Pedro seeming in serious discourse

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Walk boldly by them, I’ll come at a distance, lest he suspect us.

div2.stage: She walks by them, and looks back on them

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ha! A woman! And of an excellent mien!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: She throws a kind look back on you.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Death, tis a likely wench, and that kind look shall not be cast away. I’ll follow her.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Prithee do not.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Do not! By Heavens to the Antipodes, with such an invitation.

div2.stage: She goes out, and Willmore follows her

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: ’Tis a mad fellow for a wench.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Oh colonel, such news!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Prithee, what?

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: News that will make you laugh in spite of fortune.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: What, Blunt has had some damned trick put upon him, cheated, banged, or clapped?

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Cheated, sir, rarely cheated of all but his shirt and drawers. The unconscionable whore too turned him out before consummation, so that traversing the streets at midnight the watch found him in this fresco and conducted him home. By Heaven ’tis such a slight, and yet I durst as well have been hanged as laugh at him, or pity him! He beats all that do but ask him a question, and is in such an humor –

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Who is’t has met with this ill usage, sir?

p.seg: I’ll employ him to give Florinda time for an escape.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Who is he?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: A young countryman of ours, one that has been educated at so plentiful a rate he yet ne’er knew the want of money, and ’twill be a great jest to see how simply he’ll look without it. For my part I’ll lend him none, and the rogue knows not how to put on a borrowing face and ask first. I’ll let him see how good ’tis to play our parts whilst I play his; prithee, Fred, do go home and keep him in that posture till we come.

div2.stage: Enter Florinda from the farther end of the scene, looking behind her

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I am followed still; hah, my brother too advancing this way, good Heavens defend me from being seen by him!

div2.stage: Enter Willmore, and after him Valeria, at a little distance]

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ah! There she sails, she looks back as she were willing to be boarded, I’ll warrant her prize.

div2.stage: Enter Hellena, just as he goes out, with a page

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Hah, is not that my Captain that has a woman in chase? ’Tis not Angellica. Boy, follow those people at a distance, and bring me an account where they go in. I’ll find his haunts, and plague him everywhere. Ha, my brother!

div2.stage: Belvile, Willmore, Pedro cross the stage; Hellena runs off
Scene changes to another street; enter Florinda

sp.speaker: FLORINDA

lg.l: What shall I do? My brother now pursues me!
Will no kind power protect me from his tyranny?

sp.p: Hah, here’s a door open, I’ll venture in, since nothing can be worse than to fall into his hands! My life and honor are at stake, and my necessity has no choice.

div2.stage: Enter Valeria, and Hellena’s page peeping after Florinda

sp.speaker: PAGE
sp.p: Here she went in, I shall remember this House.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: This is Belvile’s lodgings! She’s gone in as readily as if she knew it! Hah, here’s that mad fellow again, I dare not venture in, I’ll watch my opportunity.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I have lost her hereabouts. Pox on’t, she must not escape me so!

div2.stage: Scene changes to Blunt’s chamber, discovers him sitting on a couch in his shirt and drawers, reading

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: So, now my mind’s a little at peace, since I have resolved revenge. A pox on this tailor though, for not bringing home the clothes I bespoke! And a pox of all poor cavaliers, a man can never keep a spare suit for ’em! And I shall have these rogues come in and find me naked, and then I’m undone! But I’m resolved to arm myself, the rascals shall not insult over me too much. (Puts on an old rusty sword and buff belt) Now, how like a morris dancer I am equipped. A fine lady-like whore to cheat me thus, without affording me a kindness for my money; a pox light on her, I shall never be reconciled to the sex more: she has made me as faithless as a physician, as uncharitable as a churchman, and as ill-natured as a poet. O how I’ll use all womankind hereafter! What would I give to have one of ’em within my reach now! Any mortal thing in petticoats, kind fortune, send me, and I’ll forgive thy last night’s malice! Here’s a cursed book too, “A Warning to all Young Travelers”, that can instruct me how to prevent such mischiefs now ’tis too late. Well, ’tis a rare convenient thing to read a little now and then, as well as hawk and hunt.

p.seg: This house is haunted sure, ’tis well furnished and no living thing inhabits it – Hah, a man! Heavens, how he’s attired! Sure ’tis some rope dancer, or fencing master; I tremble now for fear, and yet I must venture now to speak to him.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Hah, what’s here? Are my wishes granted? And is not that a she creature? Adsheartlikins, ’tis! What wretched thing art thou, hah!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Charitable sir, you’ve told yourself already what I am: a very wretched maid, forced by a strange unlucky accident to seek a safety here, and must be ruined if you do not grant it.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Ruined! Is there any ruin so inevitable as that which now threatens thee? Dost thou know, miserable woman, into what den of mischiefs thou art fallen? What a bliss of confusion? Hah, dost not see something in my looks that frights thy guilty soul, and makes thee wish to change that shape of woman for any humble animal, or devil? For those were safer for thee, and less mischievous.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Alas, what mean you, sir? I must confess your looks have something in ’em makes me fear; but I beseech you, as you seem a gentleman, pity a harmless virgin that takes your house for sanctuary.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Talk on, talk on, and weep too, till my faith return. Do, flatter me out of my senses again; a harmless virgin with a pox, as much one as t’other, adsheartlikins! Why, what the devil can I not be safe in my house for you? Not in my chamber? Nay, even being naked too cannot secure me. This is an impudence greater than has invaded me yet. Come, no resistance!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Dare you be so cruel?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Cruel, adsheartlikins as a galley slave or a Spanish whore; cruel, yes, I will kiss and beat thee all over; kiss, and see thee all over; thou shalt lie with me too, not that I care for the enjoyment, but to let you see I have taken deliberated malice to thee and will be revenged on one whore for the sins of another; I will smile and deceive thee, flatter thee, and beat thee, kiss and swear and lie to thee, embrace thee and rob thee as she did me, fawn on thee and strip thee stark naked, then hang thee out at my window by the heels with a paper of scurvy verses fastened to thy breast, in praise of damnable women! Come, come along!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Alas, sir, must I be sacrificed for the crimes of the most infamous of my sex? I never understood the sins you name.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Do, persuade the fool you love him, or that one of you can be just or honest; tell me I was not an easy coxcomb, or any strange impossible tale: it will be believed sooner than thy false showers or protestations. A generation of damned hypocrites, to flatter my very clothes from my back! Dissembling witches! Are these the returns you make an honest gentleman that trusts, believes, and loves you? But if I be not even with you – come along, or I shall –

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Hah, what’s here to do?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Adsheartlikins, Fred! I am glad thou art come, to be a witness of my dire revenge!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: What’s this, a person of quality too, who is upon the ramble to supply the defects of some grave impotent husband?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: No, this has another pretense, some very unfortunate accident brought her hither, to save a life pursued by I know not who or why, and forced to take sanctuary here at Fool’s Haven. Adsheartlikins, to me of all mankind for protection! Is the ass to be cajoled again, think ye? No, young one, no prayers or tears shall mitigate my rage; therefore prepare for both my pleasure of enjoyment and revenge, for I am resolved to make up my loss here on thy body, I’ll take it out in kindness and in beating.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Now, mistress of mine, what do you think of this?

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: I think he will not – dares not be so barbarous!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Have a care, Blunt, she fetched a deep sigh: she is enamored with thy shirt and drawers, she’ll strip thee even of that! There are of her calling such unconscionable baggages and such dexterous thieves they’ll flea a man, and he shall ne’er miss his skin till he feels the cold. There was a countryman of ours robbed of a row of teeth whilst he was sleeping, which the jilt made him buy again when he waked! You see, lady, how little reason we have to trust you.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Dsheartlikins, why, this is most abominable!

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Some such devils there may be, but by all that’s holy I am none such, I entered here to save a life in danger!

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: For no goodness, I’ll warrant her!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Faith, damsel, you had e’en confess the plain truth, for we are fellows not to be caught twice in the same trap; look on that wreck, a tight vessel when he set out of haven, well-trimmed and laden, and see how a female picaroon of this island of rogues has shattered him, and canst thou hope for any mercy?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: No, no, gentlewoman, come along, adsheartlikins, we must be better acquainted! We’ll both lie with her, and then let me alone to bang her.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I am ready to serve you in matters of revenge, that has a double pleasure in’t.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Well said! You hear, little one, how you are condemned by public vote to the bed within, there’s no resisting your destiny, sweetheart.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Stay, sir, I have seen you with Belvile, an English cavalier, for his sake use me kindly! You know how, sir.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Belvile! Why, yes, sweeting, we do know Belvile, and wish he were with us now, he’s a cormorant at whore and bacon, he’d have a limb or two of thee, my virgin pullet. But ’tis no matter, we’ll leave him the bones to pick.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, if you have any esteem for that Belvile, I conjure you to treat me with more gentleness, he’ll thank you for the justice.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Hark ye, Blunt, I doubt we are mistaken in this matter.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, if you find me not worth Belvile’s care, use me as you please; and that you may think I merit better treatment than you threaten. Pray take this present.

div2.stage: Gives him a ring; he looks on it

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Hum, a diamond! Why, ’tis a wonderful virtue now that lies in this ring, a mollifying virtue. Adsheartlikins, there’s more persuasive rhetoric in’t than all her sex can utter.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I begin to suspect something, and ’twould anger us vilely to be trussed up for a rape upon a maid of quality when we only believe we ruffle a harlot.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Thou art a credulous fellow, but adsheartlikins I have no faith yet. Why, my saint prattled as parlously as this does, she gave me a bracelet too, a devil on her! But I sent my man to sell it today for necessaries, and it proved as counterfeit as her vows of love.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: However let it reprieve her till we see Belvile.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: That’s hard, yet I will grant it.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Oh, sir, the colonel is just come with his new friend and a Spaniard of quality, and talks of having you to dinner with ’em.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: ’Dsheartlikins, I’m undone! I would not see ’em for the world: Hark ye, Fred, lock up the wench in your chamber.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Fear nothing, madam: whate’er he threatens, you’re safe whilst in my Hands.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: And, sirrah, upon your life, say I am not at home – or that I am asleep – or – or anything – away – I’ll prevent them coming this way.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: After a great knocking as at his chamber door, enter Blunt softly, crossing the stage in his shirt and drawers, as before

sp.speaker: WITHIN
sp.p: Ned! Ned Blunt! Ned Blunt!

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: The rogues are up in arms, ’dsheartlikins, this villainous Frederick has betrayed me, they have heard of my blessed fortune.

sp.speaker: WITHIN
sp.p: (and knocking within) Ned Blunt! Ned, Ned!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: within Why, he’s dead, sir, without dispute dead, he has not been seen today; let’s break open the door. Here, Boy –

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Ha, break open the door! ’Dsheartlikins, that mad fellow will be as good as his word!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: within Boy, bring something to force the door.

div2.stage: A great noise within at the door again

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: So, now must I speak in my own defense, I’ll try what rhetoric will do. Hold! Hold, what do you mean, gentlemen, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: within Oh rogue, art alive? Prithee open the door, and convince us.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Yes, I am alive, gentlemen, but at present a little busy.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: [within] How! Blunt grown a man of business! Come, come, open, and let’s see this miracle.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: No, no, no, no, gentlemen, ’tis no great business, but – I am – at – my devotion; ’dsheartlikins, will you not allow a man time to pray?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: [within] Turned religious! A greater wonder than the first, therefore open quickly or we shall unhinge, we shall.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: This won’t do. Why, hark ye, colonel: to tell you the plain truth, I am about a necessary affair of life. I have a wench with me – you apprehend me? The devil’s in’t if they be so uncivil as to disturb me now.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: within How, a wench! Nay, then we must enter and partake! No resistance! Unless it be your lady of quality, and then we’ll keep our distance.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: So, the business is out.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: within Come, come, lend more hands to the door – now heave altogether – (Breaks open the door) So, well done, my boys!

div2.stage: Enter Belvile, Willmore, Frederick, Pedro and Belvile’s page Boy ; Blunt looks simply, they all laugh at him, he lays his hand on his sword, and comes up to Willmore

p.seg: The jest has been carried on too long – a plague upon my taylor –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: ’Sdeath, how the whore has dressed him! Faith, sir, I’m sorry.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Are you so, sir? Keep’t to yourself then, sir, I advise you, d’ye hear? For I can as little endure your pity as his mirth.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Indeed, Willmore, thou wert a little too rough with Ned Blunt’s mistress: call a person of quality whore, and one so young, so handsome, and so eloquent! Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Hark ye, sir, you know me, and know I can be angry! Have a care, for ’dsheartlikins I can fight too, I can, sir, do you mark me? No more!

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Why so peevish, good Ned? Some disappointments, I’ll warrant. What, did the jealous count, her husband, return just in the nick?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Or the devil, sir, d’ye laugh? (They laugh) Look ye, settle me a good sober countenance, and that quickly too, or you shall know Ned Blunt is not –

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Not everybody, we know that.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Not an ass to be laughed at, sir.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Unconscionable sinner, to bring a lover so near his happiness, a vigorous passionate lover, and then not only cheat him of his moveables but his desires too.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Ah, sir, a mistress is a trifle with Blunt, he’ll have a dozen the next time he looks abroad, his eyes have charms not to be resisted. There needs no more than to expose that taking person to the view of the fair, and he leads ’em all in triumph.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Sir, though I’m a stranger to you, I’m ashamed at the rudeness of my nation; and could you learn who did it, would assist you to make an example of ’em.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Why, aye, there’s one speaks sense now, and handsomely. And let me tell you, gentlemen, I should not have showed myself like a jack pudding thus to have made you mirth, but that I have revenge within my power. For know, I have got into my possession a female who had better have fallen under any curse than the ruin I design her. ’Dsheartlikins, she assaulted me here in my own lodgings, and had doubtless committed a rape upon me had not this sword defended me.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I knew not that, but o’ my conscience thou hadst ravished her had she not redeemed herself with a ring. Let’s see’t, Blunt.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Hah, the ring I gave Florinda when we exchanged our vows! Hark ye, Blunt –

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: No whispering, good colonel, there’s a woman in the case, no whispering.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Hark ye, fool, be advised and conceal both the ring and the story for your reputation’s sake; don’t let people know what despised cullies we English are: to be cheated and abused by one whore, and another rather bribe thee than be kind to thee, is an infamy to our nation.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Come, come, where’s the wench? We’ll see her, let her be what she will, we’ll see her.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Ay, ay, let us see her, I can soon discover whether she be of quality or for your diversion.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: She’s in Fred’s custody.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: (To Frederick, who gives him the key) Come, come, the key.

p.seg: Death! What shall I do? Yet if I hinder ’em, I shall discover all.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Nay, hold there, colonel, I’ll go first.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Nay, no dispute, Ned and I have the property of her.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Damn property! Then we’ll draw cuts. (Belvile goes to whisper to Willmore) Nay, no corruption, good colonel: come, the longest sword carries her.

div2.stage: They all draw, forgetting Don Pedro, being a Spaniard, had the longest

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: I yield up my interest to you gentlemen, and that will be revenge sufficient.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: (To Pedro) The wench is yours. Pox of his Toledo, I had forgot that!

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Come, Sir, I’ll conduct you to the lady.

p.seg: To hinder him will certainly discover!

div2.stage: Willmore walking up and down out of humor

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Aye, aye, to trust our fortune to lots, a devil on’t, ’twas madness, that’s the rruth on’t.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Oh, intolerable sot!

div2.stage: Enter Florinda, running masked, Pedro after her, Willmore gazing round her

p.seg: Good Heaven, defend me from discovery!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: ’Tis but in vain to fly me, you are fallen to my lot.

p.seg: Sure she is undiscovered yet, but now I fear there is no way to bring her off.
Why, what a pox is not this my woman, the same I followed but now?

div2.stage: Pedro talking to Florinda, who walks up and down

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: As if I did not know ye, and your business here.

p.seg: Good Heaven! I fear he does indeed!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Come, pray be kind, I know you meant to be so when you entered here, for these are proper gentlemen.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: But, sir, perhaps the lady will not be imposed upon, she’ll choose her man.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: I am better bred than not to leave her choice free.

div2.stage: Enter Valeria, and is surprised at the sight of Don Pedro

p.seg: Don Pedro here! There’s no avoiding him.
Valeria! Then I’m undone!

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: (To Pedro, running to him) Oh! have I found you, sir! The strangest accident! If I had breath – to tell it!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Speak: is Florinda safe? Hellena well?

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Aye, aye, sir – Florinda – is safe – from any fears of you.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Why, where’s Florinda? Speak.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Aye, where indeed, sir? I wish I could inform you – but to hold you no longer in doubt –

p.seg: Oh, what will she say!
if you can find her out.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Dishonourable girl, she has undone my aim! Sir, you see my necessity of leaving you, and I hope you’ll pardon it: my sister, I know, will make her flight to you; and if she do, I shall expect she should be rendered back.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I shall consult my love and honor, sir.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: (To Valeria) My dear preserver, let me embrace thee!

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What the devil’s all this?

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Mystery by this light.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: Come, come, make haste and get yourselves married quickly, for your brother will return again.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: I am so surprised with fears and joys, so amazed to find you here in safety, I can scarce persuade my heart into a faith of what I see.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Hark ye, colonel, is this that mistress who has cost you so many sighs, and me so many quarrels with you?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: It is! (To Florinda) Pray give him the honor of your hand.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Thus it must be received then. (Kneels and kisses her hand) And with it give your pardon too.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: The friend to Belvile may command me anything.

p.seg: Death, would I might, ’tis a surprising beauty.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Boy, run and fetch a father instantly.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: So, now do I stand like a dog, and have not a syllable to plead my own cause with. By this hand, madam, I was never thoroughly confounded before, nor shall I ever more dare look up with confidence till you are pleased to pardon me.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, I’ll be reconciled to you on one condition, that you’ll follow the example of your friend in marrying a maid that does not hate you and whose fortune (I believe) will not be unwelcome to you.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Madam, had I no inclinations that way, I should obey your kind commands.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Who? Fred marry? He has so few inclinations for womankind that had he been possessed of Paradise he might have continued there to this day if no crime but love could have disinherited him.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Oh, I do not use to boast of my intrigues.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Boast! Why thou dost nothing but boast; and I dare swear, wer’t thou as innocent from the sin of the grape as thou art from the apple, thou mightest yet claim that right in Eden which our first parents lost by too much loving.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: I wish this lady would think me so modest a man.

sp.speaker: VALERIA
sp.p: She should be sorry then, and not like you half so well, and I should be loathe to break my word with you, which was that if your friend and mine are agreed it should be a match between you and I.

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Bear witness, colonel, ’tis a bargain.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: (To Florinda) I have a pardon to beg too; but adsheartlikins I am so out of countenance that I am a dog if I can say anything to purpose.

sp.speaker: FLORINDA
sp.p: Sir, I heartily forgive you all.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: That’s nobly said, sweet lady. Belvile, prithee present her her ring again, for I find I have not courage to approach her myself.

div2.stage: Gives him the ring, he gives it to Florinda

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Sir, I have brought the father that you sent for.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: ’Tis well, and now my dear Florinda, let’s fly to complete that mighty joy we have so long wished and sighed for. Come, Fred, you’ll follow?

sp.speaker: FREDERICK
sp.p: Your example, sir, ’twas ever my ambition in war, and must be so in love.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: And must not I see this juggling knot tied?

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: No, thou shalt do us better service, and be our guard, lest Don Pedro’s sudden return interrupt the ceremony.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Content: I’ll secure this pass.

div2.stage: Exit Belvile, Florinda, Frederick, and Valeria

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: (To Willmore) Sir, there’s a lady without would speak to you.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Conduct her in, I dare not quit my post.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: And, sir, your tailor waits you in your chamber.

sp.speaker: BLUNT
sp.p: Some comfort yet: I shall not dance naked at the wedding!

div2.stage: Enter again the Boy, conducting in Angellica in a masking habit and a vizard; Willmore runs to her]

p.seg: This can be none but my pretty gypsy!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Stand off, base villain!

div2.stage: She draws a pistol and holds to his breast

p.seg: Hah, ’tis not she!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: One thou hast injured, and who comes to kill thee for’t.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: What the devil canst thou mean?

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: By all my hopes to kill thee.

div2.stage: Holds still the pistol to his breast, he going back, she following still

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Prithee on what acquaintance? For I know thee not.

lg.l: Behold this face! So lost to thy remembrance!
And then call all thy sins about thy soul,
And let them die with thee.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Angellica!

lg.l: Yes, Traitor!
Does not thy guilty blood run shivering through thy ceins?
Hast thou no horror at this sight, that tells thee,
Thou hast not long to boast thy shameful conquest?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith no, child, my blood keeps its old ebbs and flows still, and that usual heat too, that could oblige thee with a kindness had I but opportunity.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Devil! Dost wanton with my pain, have at thy heart!

p.seg: Death, I think she’s in earnest.

l.seg: Oh if I take not heed,
My coward heart will leave me to his mercy.

lg.l: What have you, sir, to say? But should I hear thee,
Thou’ldst talk away all that is brave about me,
lg.stage: (Follows him with the pistol to his breast)
lg.l: And I have vowed thy death, by all that’s sacred.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Why, then there’s an end of a proper handsome fellow, that might have lived to have done good service yet: that’s all I can say to’t.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: (Pausingly) Yet – I would give thee – time for penitence.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, child, I thank God, I have ever took care to lead a good, sober, hopeful life, and am of a religion that teaches me to believe, I shall depart in peace.

lg.l: So will the devil: tell me,
How many poor believing fools thou hast undone?
How many hearts thou hast betrayed to ruin?
Yet these are little mischiefs to the ills
Thou’st taught mine to commit: thou’st taught it love.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, ’twas shrewdly hurt the while.

lg.l: Love, that has robbed it of its unconcern,
Of all that pride that taught me how to value it,
And in its room a mean submissive passion was conveyed
That made me humbly bow, which I ne’er did
To anything but Heaven.
Thou, perjured man, didst this, and with thy oaths
Which on thy knees thou didst devoutly make,
Softened my yielding heart; And then I was a slave,
Yet still had been content to’ve worn my chains,
Worn ’em with vanity and joy forever,
Hadst thou not broke those vows that put them on.
’Twas then I was undone.

div2.stage: All this while follows him with a pistol to his breast

lg.l: Broke my vows! Why, where hast thou lived?
Amongst the gods! For I never heard of mortal man,
That has not broke a thousand vows.
Oh, impudence!
Angellica! That beauty has been too long tempting
Not to have made a thousand lovers languish,
Who in the amorous favor, no doubt have sworn
Like me; did they all die in that faith? Still adoring?
I do not think they did.

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: No, faithless man. Had I repaid their vows, as I did thine, I would have killed the ungrateful that had abandoned me.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: This old general has quite spoiled thee: nothing makes a woman so vain as being flattered. Your old lover ever supplies the defects of age with intolerable dotage, vast charge, and that which you call constancy; and attributing all this to your own merits you domineer, and throw your favors in’s teeth, upbraiding him still with the defects of age and cuckold him as often as he deceives your expectations. But the gay, young, brisk lover that brings his equal fires and can give you dart for dart, he’ll be as nice as you sometimes.

lg.l: All this thou’st made me know, for which I hate thee.
Had I remained in innocent security,
I should have thought all men were born my slaves,
And worn my power like lightning in my eyes
To have destroyed at pleasure when offended.
But when love held the mirror, the undeceiving glass
Reflected all the weakness of my soul, and made me know,
My richest treasure being lost, my honor,
All the remaining spoil could not be worth
The conqueror’s care or value.
Oh, how I fell like a long-worshiped idol,
Discovering all the cheat!
Would not the incense and rich sacrifice,
Which blind devotion offered at my altars,
Have fallen to thee?
Why woudst thou then destroy my fancied power?
By Heaven, thou art brave, and I admire thee strangely.
I wish I were that dull, that constant thing,
Which thou woudst have, and nature never meant me.
I must, like cheerful birds, sing in all groves,
And perch on every bough,
Billing the next kind she that flies to meet me.
Yet after all could build my nest with thee,
Thither repairing when I’d loved my round,
And still reserve a tributary flame.
To gain your credit, I’ll pay you back your charity
And be obliged for nothing but for love.

div2.stage: Offers her a purse of gold

lg.l: Oh that thou wert in earnest!
So mean a thought of me
Would turn my rage to scorn, and I should pity thee
And give thee leave to live,
Which for the public safety of our sex,
And my own private injuries, I dare not do.
Prepare –
– I will no more be tempted with replies.
Sure –

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Another word will damn thee! I’ve heard thee talk too long.

div2.stage: She follows him with a pistol ready to shoot: he retires still amazed
Enter Don Antonio, his arm in a scarf, and lays hold on the pistol

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Hah! Angellica!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Antonio! What devil brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Love and curiosity, seeing your coach at door. Let me disarm you of this unbecoming instrument of death. (Takes away the pistol) Amongst the number of your slaves, was there not one worthy the honor to have fought your quarrel? Who are you, sir, that are so very wretched to merit death from her?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: One, sir, that could have made a better end of an amorous quarrel without you than with you.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Sure, ’tis some rival! Hah, the very man took down her picture yesterday, the very same that set on me last night; blessed opportunity!

sp.speaker: ANGELLICA
sp.p: Hold, you’re mistaken, Sir.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: By Heaven, the very same! Sir, what pretensions have you to this lady?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Sir, I don’t use to be examined, and am ill at all disputes but this.

lg.l: (To Willmore) Oh, hold! you see he’s armed with certain death!
And you, Antonio, I command you hold,
By all the passion you’ve so lately vowed me.

div2.stage: Enter Don Pedro, sees Antonio, and stays

p.seg: Hah, Antonio! And Angellica!

lg.l: When I refuse obedience to your will,
May you destroy me with your mortal hate.
By all that’s holy, I adore you so,
That even my rival, who has charms enough
To make him fall a victim to my jealousy,
Shall live, nay, and have leave to love on still.

p.seg: What’s this I hear?

lg.l: (Pointing to Willmore) Ah thus, ’twas thus he talked, and I believed. Antonio, yesterday,
I’d not have sold my interest in his heart
For all the sword has won and lost in battle.
To Willmore But now, to show my utmost of contempt,
I give thee life, which if thou wouldst preserve;
Live where my eyes may never see thee more,
Live to undo someone whose soul may prove
So bravely constant to revenge my love.

div2.stage: Goes out; Antonio follows, but Pedro pulls him back

lg.l: Antonio, stay.
Don Pedro!
What coward fear was that prevented thee
From meeting me this morning on the Molo?
Meet thee?
Yes, me; I was the man that dared thee to’t.
Hast thou so often seen me fight in war,
To find no better cause to excuse my absence?
I sent my sword and one to do thee right,
Finding myself uncapable to use a sword.
But ’twas Florinda’s quarrel that we fought,
And you to show how little you esteemed her,
Sent me your rival, giving him your interest.
But I have found the cause of this affront,
But when I meet you fit for the dispute,
I’ll tell you my resentment.
I shall be ready, sir, ere long to do you reason.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: If I could find Florinda, now whilst my anger’s high, I think I should be kind and give her to Belvile in revenge.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, Sir, I know not what you would do, but I believe the priest within has been so kind.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: How! My sister married?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: I hope by this time she is, and bedded too, or he has not my longings about him.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Dares he do thus? Does he not fear my power?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Faith, not at all. If you will go in, and thank him for the favor he has done your sister, so. If not, sir, my power’s greater in this house than yours: I have a damned surly crew here that will keep you till the next tide, and then clap you and board my prize. My ship lies but a league off the Molo, and we shall show your donship a damned Tramontana rover’s trick.

p.seg: This rogue’s in some new mischief – hah, Pedro returned!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Colonel Belvile, I hear you have married my sister.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: You have heard truth then, sir.

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: Have I so? Then, sir, I wish you joy.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: By this embrace I do, and I glad on’t.

sp.speaker: BELVILE
sp.p: Are you in earnest?

sp.speaker: PEDRO
sp.p: By our long friendship and my obligations to thee, I am. The sudden change I’ll give you reasons for anon. Come, lead me into my sister, that she may know I now approve her choice.

div2.stage: Willmore goes to follow them; Enter Hellena as before in boy’s clothes, and pulls him back

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Ha, my gypsy! Now a thousand blessings on thee for this kindness. Egad, child, I was e’en in despair of ever seeing thee again; my friends are all provided for within, each man his kind woman.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Hah! I thought they had served me some such trick.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: And I was e’en resolved to go aboard, condemn myself to my lone cabin and the thoughts of thee.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And could you have left me behind? Would you have been so ill-natured?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Why, ’twould have broke my heart, child. But since we are met again, I defy foul weather to part us.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: And would you be a faithful friend now, if a maid should trust you?

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: For a friend I cannot promise, thou art of a form so excellent, a face and humor too good for cold dull friendship. I am parlously afraid of being in love, child, and you have not forgot how severely you have used me.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: That’s all one, such usage you must still look for, to find out all your haunts, to rail at you to all that love you, till I have made you love only me in your own defense, because nobody else will love.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: But hast thou no better quality to recommend thyself by?

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Faith none, captain. Why, ’twill be the greater charity to take me for thy mistress: I am a lone child, a kind of orphan lover, and why I should die a maid, and in a captain’s hands too, I do not understand.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
sp.p: Egad, I was never clawed away with broadsides from any female before; thou hast one virtue I adore: good nature. I hate a coy demure mistress, she’s as troublesome as a colt, I’ll break none. No, give me a mad mistress when mewed, and in flying on[e] I dare trust upon the wing that whilst she’s kind will come to the lure.

sp.speaker: HELLENA
sp.p: Nay, as kind as you will, good Captain, whilst it lasts, but let’s lose no time.

sp.speaker: WILLMORE
